/stories/characters/draupadi/.intro: Draupadi is born fully grown from a sacrificial fire lit by her father King Drupada, who wanted a son to defeat his enemy Drona. She is won by Arjuna in an archery contest and becomes the wife of all five Pandava brothers. During a rigged dice game, her enemies try to strip her in public, and in the best-known telling Krishna saves her by making her sari endless.

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: the fire-born princess who marries all five Pandava brothers

whoIsWho.name: Drupada
whoIsWho.role: the king whose sacrifice against Drona produces her

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the Pandava archer who wins her hand

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: in the popular telling, saves her from being stripped in the assembly hall

whoIsWho.name: Duhshasana
whoIsWho.role: the Kaurava prince who drags her by the hair and tries to strip her

/stories/characters/draupadi/.whyItMatters: Her humiliation in the assembly hall is treated in the epic as the moral turning point that makes the war between the Kauravas and Pandavas unavoidable.

/stories/characters/drupada/.intro: King Drupada of Panchala breaks a boyhood promise to share his kingdom with his friend Drona, and when Drona later takes revenge by seizing half his land, Drupada holds a fire sacrifice to gain a son who can kill Drona. The sacrifice produces two children: Dhrishtadyumna, born to kill Drona, and Draupadi, born to marry the Pandavas.

whoIsWho.name: Drupada
whoIsWho.role: king of Panchala whose broken friendship with Drona sets off the feud

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: the poor priest turned Kuru teacher, once Drupada's boyhood friend

whoIsWho.name: Dhrishtadyumna
whoIsWho.role: Drupada's fire-born son, destined to kill Drona

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: Drupada's fire-born daughter, who marries the five Pandavas

/stories/characters/drupada/.whyItMatters: His pursuit of revenge through ritual sets in motion the births and alliances that lead to the war at Kurukshetra and, in the end, the destruction of his own family line.

/stories/mahabharata/01-adi-parva/.intro: The Adi Parva is the opening book of the Mahabharata. It tells how the Kuru royal family began, how the Kaurava and Pandava cousins were born and raised, how the Pandavas survived an attempted murder by fire, and how they won Draupadi as their shared wife and founded the city of Indraprastha.

whoIsWho.name: Bhishma
whoIsWho.role: prince who gives up the throne and takes a vow of lifelong celibacy

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: the teacher of the Kaurava and Pandava princes

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: the princess born from fire who becomes the shared wife of the five Pandava brothers

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the Pandava archer who wins Draupadi's hand

whoIsWho.name: Duryodhana
whoIsWho.role: the eldest Kaurava prince, born amid bad omens, and rival of the Pandavas

/stories/mahabharata/01-adi-parva/.whyItMatters: It lays out the family history, rivalries, and marriages that make the later war between the Kauravas and Pandavas feel inevitable.

/stories/samudra-manthana/.intro: The gods and demons join forces to churn the cosmic ocean of milk using a mountain as a rod and a giant serpent as a rope, hoping to bring up the nectar of immortality. Many treasures rise from the ocean before the nectar itself appears, and Vishnu has to trick the demons so the gods alone drink it.

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: takes the form of a turtle to support the mountain, then becomes the enchantress Mohini to secure the nectar for the gods

whoIsWho.name: Indra
whoIsWho.role: king of the gods, restored to power once the gods regain the nectar

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: swallows a deadly poison that surfaces during the churning, turning his throat blue

whoIsWho.name: Lakshmi
whoIsWho.role: goddess of fortune who rises from the ocean during the churning

whoIsWho.name: Bali
whoIsWho.role: leader of the demons in this telling

/stories/samudra-manthana/.whyItMatters: The churning explains the origin of several major gods, sacred objects, and the ongoing rivalry between gods and demons.

/stories/vamana-bali/.intro: Vishnu is born as a small brahmin dwarf named Vamana and asks Bali, a demon-king famous for never refusing a request, for just three paces of land. Bali agrees even after his teacher warns him not to, and Vamana grows into a giant who covers the earth and sky in two steps, then gently sends Bali to rule the netherworld instead of punishing him.

whoIsWho.name: Vamana
whoIsWho.role: the dwarf form Vishnu takes to approach Bali

whoIsWho.name: Bali
whoIsWho.role: the demon king who keeps his promise even when it costs him everything

whoIsWho.name: Shukra
whoIsWho.role: Bali's teacher, who warns him not to grant the gift of land

whoIsWho.name: Prahlada
whoIsWho.role: Bali's grandfather, who pleads for him

/stories/vamana-bali/.whyItMatters: The story became the origin legend of the Kerala harvest festival Onam, where Bali is honored as a beloved former king who returns once a year.

/stories/varaha-hiranyaksha/.intro: When the demon Hiranyaksha drags the earth down into the cosmic ocean, Vishnu takes the form of a giant boar named Varaha, dives in to rescue her, and fights the demon in a battle said to last a thousand years before killing him and lifting the earth back into place on his tusks.

whoIsWho.name: Varaha
whoIsWho.role: Vishnu's boar form, who rescues the earth

whoIsWho.name: Hiranyaksha
whoIsWho.role: the demon who drags the earth into the cosmic ocean

whoIsWho.name: Bhudevi
whoIsWho.role: the earth goddess Varaha lifts to safety

/stories/varaha-hiranyaksha/.whyItMatters: The story explains why the present cosmic age is named the Shveta-Varaha age, "the White Boar age," after this rescue.

/stories/prahlada-narasimha/.intro: The demon king Hiranyakashipu wins a boon that makes him almost impossible to kill, then turns on his own son Prahlada for worshipping Vishnu instead of him. When Hiranyakashipu demands to know if Vishnu is even in a palace pillar, Vishnu bursts out as Narasimha, a being that is neither man nor beast, and kills him at twilight on a doorway threshold, satisfying every condition of the boon.

whoIsWho.name: Hiranyakashipu
whoIsWho.role: the demon king who wins near-invincibility and persecutes his son

whoIsWho.name: Prahlada
whoIsWho.role: his son, a devoted child who survives every attempt to kill him

whoIsWho.name: Narasimha
whoIsWho.role: the half-man, half-lion form Vishnu takes to kill Hiranyakashipu

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the god who becomes Narasimha

/stories/prahlada-narasimha/.whyItMatters: The story is often read as showing that no boon or clever wording can outwit true devotion, since Vishnu finds a way through every loophole in Hiranyakashipu's protection.

/stories/jaya-vijaya/.intro: Jaya and Vijaya are Vishnu's two gatekeepers in his heavenly home, Vaikuntha. When they rudely turn away four child-sages at the gate, the sages curse them to be born as enemies of Vishnu three times over. Rather than face seven lifetimes apart from him as devotees, the two choose three lives as demons killed by Vishnu's own hand each time, so they can return to him faster.

whoIsWho.name: Jaya
whoIsWho.role: one of Vishnu's two gatekeepers, reborn three times as a demon and killed each time by Vishnu

whoIsWho.name: Vijaya
whoIsWho.role: the other gatekeeper, sharing the same three-life curse alongside Jaya

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the god who kills each pair and welcomes them home

whoIsWho.name: the four Kumaras
whoIsWho.role: the child-sages who curse the gatekeepers after being turned away

/stories/jaya-vijaya/.whyItMatters: The curse ties together several of Vishnu's most famous demon-slayings, showing they are really the same two souls working their way back to him across three ages.

/deities/dashavatara/.intro: The Dashavatara is the traditional list of Vishnu's ten major descents to earth, each appearing in a different age to restore order when evil grows too strong. The list runs from Matsya the fish at the dawn of this world-cycle to Kalki, a rider still to come at the end of the current age.

whoIsWho.name: Matsya
whoIsWho.role: the fish who saves Manu and all living seeds from a great flood

whoIsWho.name: Varaha
whoIsWho.role: the boar who rescues the earth from the depths

whoIsWho.name: Narasimha
whoIsWho.role: the man-lion who kills the demon Hiranyakashipu

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: the exiled prince of the Ramayana

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the eighth descent, central to the Mahabharata and the Bhagavad Gita

/deities/dashavatara/.whyItMatters: The Dashavatara is the framework most Hindus use to place the well-known stories of Rama, Krishna, and the other avatars on a single timeline.

/stories/matsya-pralaya/.intro: Vishnu takes the form of a fish to warn a righteous man, Manu, that a great flood is coming. The fish grows enormous, and Manu ties his boat to its horn so it can tow him to safety along with seeds of every living thing and seven great sages, so life can begin again after the flood.

whoIsWho.name: Matsya
whoIsWho.role: the fish form Vishnu takes to save Manu

whoIsWho.name: Manu
whoIsWho.role: the righteous man who survives the flood and refounds humanity

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the god who becomes Matsya

/stories/matsya-pralaya/.whyItMatters: The story is the first of Vishnu's ten great descents and explains why Manu is honored as the ancestor of the current age of humanity.

/beings/garuda/.intro: Garuda is the golden eagle-king who becomes Vishnu's mount. He is born from an egg to eventually win freedom for his mother, who has been enslaved by her sister Kadru, mother of the serpents. To free her, Garuda journeys to steal the nectar of immortality from the gods, and his lasting hostility toward snakes begins here.

whoIsWho.name: Garuda
whoIsWho.role: the giant eagle who becomes Vishnu's mount

whoIsWho.name: Vinata
whoIsWho.role: Garuda's mother, enslaved after losing a bet to her sister

whoIsWho.name: Kadru
whoIsWho.role: Vinata's sister, mother of the serpents

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: grants Garuda immortality and makes him his mount

/beings/garuda/.whyItMatters: Garuda's rivalry with serpents and his role as Vishnu's mount make him one of the most widely recognized figures in Hindu art, and the national emblem of countries such as Indonesia and Thailand.

/stories/mohini-avatara/.intro: Mohini is the only female form Vishnu takes among his many avatars. He becomes her to trick greedy demons out of the nectar of immortality after the churning of the ocean, serving it only to the gods. In a later, more folk-based story, Mohini's beauty also leads a demon named Bhasmasura to accidentally destroy himself.

whoIsWho.name: Mohini
whoIsWho.role: Vishnu's only female avatar

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the god who becomes Mohini

whoIsWho.name: Bhasmasura
whoIsWho.role: in a popular but non-scriptural story, a demon tricked into killing himself while dancing with Mohini

/stories/mohini-avatara/.whyItMatters: The Mohini stories teach that clever deception, not force, can be as powerful a tool as any weapon when used to protect the world's order.

/stories/bhasmasura-and-vrikasura/.intro: These are two versions of one warning story: a demon devoted to Shiva wins power to burn to ash anyone he touches on the head, then tries to test it on Shiva. In the older, scripture-based version the demon Vrikasura is tricked into touching his own head by Vishnu disguised as a student; in the popular version the demon Bhasmasura is tricked the same way by Vishnu disguised as Mohini.

whoIsWho.name: Vrikasura
whoIsWho.role: the demon in the scriptural version, son of Shakuni, who wins the deadly boon from Shiva

whoIsWho.name: Bhasmasura
whoIsWho.role: the demon in the popular, non-scriptural version, who wins the same boon

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: grants the fatal boon and then has to flee from it

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: tricks the demon into destroying himself, appearing as a student in one version and as Mohini in the other

/stories/bhasmasura-and-vrikasura/.whyItMatters: Both versions warn that a boon granted without judging the person receiving it can endanger even the god who gave it.

/stories/kaliya-mardana/.intro: The young Krishna dives into a pool of the Yamuna river to confront Kaliya, a giant poisonous serpent whose venom has been killing people, animals, and plants nearby. After Kaliya coils around him and nearly crushes him, Krishna grows larger, then dances on the serpent's many hoods until Kaliya surrenders, and Krishna banishes him from the river instead of killing him.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the boy who subdues Kaliya

whoIsWho.name: Kaliya
whoIsWho.role: the poisonous serpent living in the Yamuna

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's brother, who reassures the frightened onlookers

whoIsWho.name: Kaliya's wives
whoIsWho.role: plead with Krishna to spare their husband

/stories/kaliya-mardana/.whyItMatters: The story is one of the most depicted scenes in Indian art and dance, showing Krishna as a boy already master over even the most dangerous forces of nature.

/stories/krishna-lila/.intro: This page traces Krishna's life after his childhood in Vrindavan. He kills the tyrant king Kamsa, who once tried to have him killed as a baby, marries several wives, and founds the city of Dwarka. He later guides the Pandavas as Arjuna's charioteer in the Mahabharata war, and eventually dies from an arrow wound just before the sea swallows his city.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the eighth avatar of Vishnu, whose life this page covers from childhood's end to death

whoIsWho.name: Kamsa
whoIsWho.role: the tyrant king of Mathura whom Krishna kills

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's elder brother, who dies around the same time as him

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the Pandava warrior Krishna serves as charioteer and counselor

whoIsWho.name: Radha
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's beloved in later devotional tradition, though she is not named in the oldest version of these stories

/stories/krishna-lila/.whyItMatters: This page traces the arc of Krishna's whole life as told across the Puranas, from divine child to world-shaping king to his quiet death, which traditionally marks the start of the present age, Kali Yuga.

/stories/krishna-balya-lila/.intro: This page tells the stories of Krishna's earliest years as a baby and toddler in the cowherd village of Gokula, before his family moves to Vrindavan. As an infant he survives assassination attempts by demons sent by the tyrant king Kamsa, and as a toddler he pulls down two cursed trees, freeing two former celestial beings trapped inside them.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the divine infant and toddler at the center of these stories

whoIsWho.name: Putana
whoIsWho.role: a demoness sent to poison baby Krishna with her milk, but is instead killed by him

whoIsWho.name: Yashoda
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's foster mother, who once sees the entire universe inside his mouth

whoIsWho.name: Kamsa
whoIsWho.role: the tyrant king who sends demons to kill the infant Krishna

/stories/krishna-balya-lila/.whyItMatters: These childhood stories are loved for showing tenderness and divine power together, letting devotees imagine God as approachable as their own baby.

/deities/devi-mahatmya-and-the-great-god.intro: The Devi Mahatmya is a scripture that tells three stories in which the Great Goddess defeats demons that no male god can stop, showing that the divine feminine power, Shakti, is the ultimate source behind all the gods. Its most famous section describes the buffalo-demon Mahishasura, defeated by the goddess Durga after being formed from the combined light and weapons of all the male gods.

whoIsWho.name: Durga
whoIsWho.role: the many-armed goddess formed from the gods' combined power, who kills the buffalo-demon Mahishasura

whoIsWho.name: Mahishasura
whoIsWho.role: the buffalo-shaped demon who conquers heaven and can only be killed by a woman

whoIsWho.name: Kali
whoIsWho.role: a fierce, dark form that bursts from the goddess's brow during battle

whoIsWho.name: Shiva, Vishnu, and Brahma
whoIsWho.role: the three male gods who, in this text, need the Goddess's power to defeat the demons they cannot beat alone

/deities/devi-mahatmya-and-the-great-god.whyItMatters: The text is the founding scripture of Shakta worship, the tradition that treats the Goddess, not any male god, as the supreme reality, and it is recited in full every year during the festival of Navratri.

/deities/sati-daksha-and-parvati/.intro: The Goddess is born once as Sati, daughter of King Daksha, and marries Shiva against her father's wishes. When Daksha insults Shiva at a great sacrifice, Sati gives up her own body in grief and anger, and Shiva's followers destroy the sacrifice in revenge. The Goddess is later reborn as Parvati, daughter of the Himalayas, and wins Shiva back as her husband through years of devoted practice.

whoIsWho.name: Sati
whoIsWho.role: the Goddess's first life, daughter of Daksha, who gives up her body after her father insults Shiva

whoIsWho.name: Daksha
whoIsWho.role: the king who despises his son-in-law Shiva and is later punished for it

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: the ascetic god who marries Sati and, after her death, is drawn back into married life as Parvati's husband

whoIsWho.name: Parvati
whoIsWho.role: the Goddess reborn as the daughter of the Himalaya, who wins Shiva through austerity

/deities/sati-daksha-and-parvati/.whyItMatters: The story explains why the Goddess has two lives, and it is the origin story behind the network of Shakti Pitha shrines said to mark where pieces of Sati's body fell.

/stories/tarakasura-vadha/.intro: The demon Tarakasura wins a boon that only a son of Shiva can kill him — seemingly impossible, since Shiva has withdrawn from the world in grief after his wife Sati's death. To make the birth happen, the gods arrange Shiva's marriage to Parvati and send the love god Kama to stir his desire, though Shiva burns Kama to ash. Their son Skanda leads the gods and kills Tarakasura.

whoIsWho.name: Tarakasura
whoIsWho.role: the demon whose clever boon can only be undone by a child of Shiva

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: the ascetic god whose remarriage and fatherhood become the gods' only hope

whoIsWho.name: Parvati
whoIsWho.role: the goddess who marries Shiva and becomes Skanda's mother

whoIsWho.name: Skanda (Kartikeya)
whoIsWho.role: the war-god son of Shiva and Parvati, born to kill Tarakasura

whoIsWho.name: Kama
whoIsWho.role: the love god burned to ash by Shiva while trying to awaken his desire

/stories/tarakasura-vadha/.whyItMatters: The story turns Shiva's return to married life into a cosmic necessity, showing the tradition's belief that even the greatest renunciate has world-saving duties as a householder and father.

/stories/gajendra-moksha/.intro: An elephant king named Gajendra is seized by a crocodile while bathing. After a struggle lasting a thousand years leaves him too weak to fight on, he stops struggling and instead surrenders completely in prayer to Vishnu. Vishnu flies to the lake at once, kills the crocodile, and frees the elephant, revealing that both animals were once cursed beings from earlier lives.

whoIsWho.name: Gajendra
whoIsWho.role: the elephant king who surrenders to Vishnu after being seized by a crocodile

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the god who rescues Gajendra the moment he calls out in total surrender

whoIsWho.name: Indradyumna
whoIsWho.role: the king Gajendra used to be, cursed to be reborn as an elephant

/stories/gajendra-moksha/.whyItMatters: The story is treated as the model example of total surrender to God, still recited daily by many devotees who see themselves in Gajendra's helplessness.

/deities/ganesha-and-kartikeya/.intro: This page tells the stories of Shiva and Parvati's two sons. Ganesha, the elephant-headed god, is created by Parvati, then accidentally beheaded by Shiva and revived with an elephant's head; he later wins a race against his brother by simply circling his parents instead of the world. Kartikeya, the six-faced war god, is born through fire and the river Ganga so he can grow up and kill the demon Tarakasura.

whoIsWho.name: Ganesha
whoIsWho.role: the elephant-headed god of beginnings, formed by Parvati

whoIsWho.name: Kartikeya (also called Skanda or Murugan)
whoIsWho.role: the six-faced war god, son of Shiva and Parvati, born to kill Tarakasura

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: the father who accidentally beheads Ganesha, then restores him with an elephant's head

whoIsWho.name: Parvati
whoIsWho.role: the mother of both sons

/deities/ganesha-and-kartikeya/.whyItMatters: These two gods are among the most worshipped in India, Ganesha invoked at the start of any undertaking and Kartikeya especially honored as Murugan in South India.

/stories/ganesha-gita/.intro: The Ganesha Gita is a lesser-known scripture in which the elephant-headed god Ganesha, not Krishna, teaches a king named Varenya the same core lessons as the Bhagavad Gita. Most of its verses are closely adapted from the Bhagavad Gita itself, simply replacing Krishna's name with Ganesha's, to argue that Ganesha, too, is the Supreme Being.

whoIsWho.name: Ganesha
whoIsWho.role: the teacher in this scripture, cast in the role Krishna plays in the Bhagavad Gita

whoIsWho.name: King Varenya
whoIsWho.role: the troubled king who receives Ganesha's teaching

/stories/ganesha-gita/.whyItMatters: The text is the key scripture used by the Ganapatya tradition, which worships Ganesha as the highest reality above all other gods.

/stories/markandeya/.intro: Markandeya is a boy fated to die at sixteen, but his devotion to Shiva saves him. When Death comes for him as he clings to a Shiva shrine, Shiva bursts out and defeats Death, granting the boy eternal life. Because he never dies, Markandeya later survives the total dissolution of the universe and sees the infant Vishnu resting on a leaf on the cosmic ocean.

whoIsWho.name: Markandeya
whoIsWho.role: the boy granted eternal youth who later survives the end of the universe

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: defeats Death to save his young devotee

whoIsWho.name: Yama
whoIsWho.role: the god of death who comes to take Markandeya

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: appears to Markandeya as a divine infant during the cosmic dissolution

/stories/markandeya/.whyItMatters: Markandeya's two stories link Shiva's power over death and Vishnu's role as keeper of the cosmos through destruction, making him one of the few figures honored across different Hindu traditions as a witness to both.

/stories/parashurama/.intro: Parashurama is a warrior-priest and an avatar of Vishnu whose father's wish-granting cow is stolen by a king; after killing that king, the king's sons kill his father in revenge, so Parashurama wipes out the entire warrior class twenty-one times over. Unlike other avatars, he never dies, living on long enough to test the young Rama's strength, teach weapons to Bhishma, Drona, and Karna, and train the future avatar Kalki.

whoIsWho.name: Parashurama
whoIsWho.role: the immortal warrior-priest avatar of Vishnu who wields an axe

whoIsWho.name: Jamadagni
whoIsWho.role: his father, a sage murdered after a king steals the family's wish-cow

whoIsWho.name: Kartavirya Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the thousand-armed king who steals the cow and is killed by Parashurama

whoIsWho.name: Karna
whoIsWho.role: one of the warriors Parashurama later trains, whom he also curses

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: the later avatar whose strength Parashurama tests by challenging him to string a bow

/stories/parashurama/.whyItMatters: As the only avatar who never dies, Parashurama becomes the living link connecting the ages of Rama, Krishna, and the future Kalki.

/stories/karna/.intro: Karna is secretly the eldest son of Kunti, born to the sun god before her marriage and abandoned in a basket on a river, then raised by a humble charioteer family. Despite being a match for Arjuna in skill, he is mocked for his low birth, becomes the loyal friend of the Pandavas' rival Duryodhana, and dies fighting his own unacknowledged brothers at Kurukshetra, undone by a chain of curses.

whoIsWho.name: Karna
whoIsWho.role: Kunti's secret eldest son, a warrior equal to Arjuna

whoIsWho.name: Kunti
whoIsWho.role: his mother, who abandons him as a baby and only reveals the truth after his death

whoIsWho.name: Duryodhana
whoIsWho.role: the Kaurava prince who befriends and honors Karna when others mock him

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: Karna's unacknowledged half-brother and greatest rival, who kills him in the war

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: reveals Karna's true parentage to him before the war, and reminds him of his own past cruelties, such as the killing of Abhimanyu, just before his death

/stories/karna/.whyItMatters: Karna's story is often read as the Mahabharata's sharpest statement on how birth and caste can waste even the greatest talent and loyalty.

/stories/sudama-kuchela/.intro: Sudama, also called Kuchela, is a desperately poor childhood friend of Krishna who travels to Krishna's city carrying only a small gift of flattened rice, too embarrassed to ask for help. Krishna welcomes him like royalty, eats the humble gift with joy, and afterward secretly transforms Sudama's home into a palace, without Sudama ever having to ask for anything.

whoIsWho.name: Sudama (Kuchela)
whoIsWho.role: the poor brahmin friend who visits Krishna empty-handed but full of love

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: welcomes his poor friend as an equal and rewards him with unasked-for wealth

/stories/sudama-kuchela/.whyItMatters: The story teaches that God values the love behind a gift over its size, and rewards true devotion even when nothing is asked in return.

/stories/govardhana-dharana/.intro: As a boy, Krishna convinces the cowherds of his village to stop their yearly offering to the storm god Indra and worship the local hill and cattle instead. Furious at being snubbed, Indra sends a flood to destroy the village, so Krishna lifts the entire hill on one finger and holds it up like an umbrella for seven days until Indra gives up and apologizes.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the boy who redirects worship away from Indra and then lifts the hill to protect his village

whoIsWho.name: Indra
whoIsWho.role: the storm god who sends a flood in anger, then submits to Krishna

whoIsWho.name: Nanda
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's foster father, one of the village elders persuaded to change the sacrifice

/stories/govardhana-dharana/.whyItMatters: The story is still celebrated every year as Govardhana Puja, when people build a small hill of food to reenact Krishna's redirection of worship from the sky-god to the land that actually sustains life.

/deities/ganga/.intro: Ganga is the river goddess who flows through heaven, earth, and the underworld, and whose water is believed to wash away sin and free the dead. She descends to earth after generations of prayer by kings whose 60,000 ancestors were burned to ash by a sage's fiery glance, and Shiva breaks the force of her fall by catching her in his hair before releasing her as the Ganges.

whoIsWho.name: Ganga
whoIsWho.role: the goddess and river said to purify all who touch or remember her

whoIsWho.name: Bhagiratha
whoIsWho.role: the king whose long penance finally brings Ganga down from heaven

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: catches Ganga's fall in his matted hair to protect the earth

whoIsWho.name: Sagara
whoIsWho.role: the ancestor-king whose 60,000 sons are burned to ash and need Ganga's water to reach heaven

whoIsWho.name: Bhishma
whoIsWho.role: in the Mahabharata, Ganga's mortal son by King Shantanu

/deities/ganga/.whyItMatters: Ganga's story explains why bathing in the Ganges, and being cremated on its banks, are treated as among the most powerful ways to purify a soul in Hindu practice.

/stories/dilipa-nandini/.intro: King Dilipa and his queen cannot have children because Dilipa once failed to bow to a sacred wish-granting cow, the sage Vasishtha tells them. To lift the curse, the couple serve the cow's daughter, Nandini, with devotion for three weeks. When a lion attacks Nandini, Dilipa offers his body to save her; the lion vanishes, revealing a test, and Nandini rewards his selflessness with the birth of a son, Raghu.

whoIsWho.name: Dilipa
whoIsWho.role: the childless king who serves the cow Nandini to lift a curse

whoIsWho.name: Nandini
whoIsWho.role: the wish-cow who tests Dilipa's devotion and grants him a son

whoIsWho.name: Vasishtha
whoIsWho.role: the sage who diagnoses the cause of the king's childlessness

whoIsWho.name: Raghu
whoIsWho.role: the son born from the boon, who becomes the dynasty's namesake

/stories/dilipa-nandini/.whyItMatters: The story is the opening set piece of the poet Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, and establishes selfless devotion as the standard by which the dynasty's later kings, including Rama, are measured.

/lineages/sagara/.intro: Sagara is an ancestor-king of Rama's dynasty who is born after his exiled father dies in the forest, while his mother carries him for years, poisoned by a jealous rival wife. Sagara reclaims his family's throne, then performs a great horse sacrifice; when the sacrificial horse is stolen and hidden underground, his 60,000 sons dig down searching for it, insult the meditating sage guarding it, and are burned to ashes.

whoIsWho.name: Sagara
whoIsWho.role: the emperor born of a poisoned pregnancy who later fathers 60,000 sons

whoIsWho.name: Kapila
whoIsWho.role: the sage whose glance burns Sagara's 60,000 sons to ash

whoIsWho.name: Bhagiratha
whoIsWho.role: Sagara's descendant, who later brings the Ganga down from heaven to free the ashes

whoIsWho.name: Keshini and Sumati
whoIsWho.role: Sagara's two queens, one who bears the single heir and one who bears the 60,000 sons

/lineages/sagara/.whyItMatters: Sagara's story explains why the ocean is called "sagara" in Sanskrit, and sets up the far more famous tale of how the Ganges river came to earth.

/stories/tripura-dahana/.intro: Three demon brothers win three flying fortresses that can only be destroyed by a single arrow fired at the one moment in a thousand years when all three cities line up. When the brothers' rule turns tyrannical, the gods lend their own bodies and weapons to build Shiva a cosmic chariot, and Shiva destroys all three cities with one shot.

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: the god who destroys the three cities with a single arrow

whoIsWho.name: Tarakaksha, Vidyunmali, and Kamalaksha
whoIsWho.role: the three demon brothers who rule the flying cities

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: becomes the arrow in Shiva's cosmic weapon, and separately sends a deceiver to weaken the demons' protection

whoIsWho.name: Brahma
whoIsWho.role: serves as Shiva's charioteer for the battle

/stories/tripura-dahana/.whyItMatters: The story is the central proof-text for Shiva's supremacy in Shaiva tradition, showing every other god reduced to a part of his weapon.

/stories/kamsa-vadha/.intro: Krishna leaves his cowherd village and travels to the city of Mathura to fulfill a prophecy that he will kill his tyrant uncle, King Kamsa. Along the way he breaks Kamsa's ceremonial bow, kills a rampaging elephant and two champion wrestlers sent to murder him, and finally drags Kamsa down and kills him, restoring the rightful king, his grandfather Ugrasena, to the throne.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the young man who kills the tyrant Kamsa as foretold

whoIsWho.name: Kamsa
whoIsWho.role: the tyrant king of Mathura who tries to have Krishna killed

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's brother, who fights alongside him in Mathura

whoIsWho.name: Ugrasena
whoIsWho.role: Kamsa's father, restored to the throne after his son's death

/stories/kamsa-vadha/.whyItMatters: Kamsa's death marks the turning point where Krishna leaves his life as a cowherd behind and becomes a prince and future king.

/stories/narakasura-vadha/.intro: The demon king Narakasura, son of the earth goddess, imprisons over 16,000 women and steals treasures from the gods, so Krishna flies to his fortress on the bird Garuda with his wife Satyabhama, and kills him. Krishna then marries all the freed women so they can live with honor, and the story becomes the origin legend for Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before Diwali.

whoIsWho.name: Narakasura
whoIsWho.role: the demon king who imprisons thousands of women and is killed by Krishna

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: kills Narakasura and marries the rescued women to restore their honor

whoIsWho.name: Satyabhama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's wife, who fights beside him in the battle

whoIsWho.name: Bhumi (the earth goddess)
whoIsWho.role: Narakasura's mother, who appears after his death to ask Krishna to protect her grandson

/stories/narakasura-vadha/.whyItMatters: The story is the reason Naraka Chaturdashi is celebrated with oil baths and lamps the night before Diwali, especially as the main Diwali legend in South India.

/stories/syamantaka-jewel/.intro: When a magical sun-gem goes missing after its wearer is killed by a lion, Krishna is wrongly accused of stealing it and sets out to clear his name. His search leads him into a cave where he fights the bear-king Jambavan for many days, wins both the jewel and Jambavan's daughter as a bride, and later marries a second wife, Satyabhama, as an apology from the jewel's original owner.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: falsely accused of theft, who investigates and clears his own name

whoIsWho.name: Jambavan
whoIsWho.role: the bear-king who takes the jewel, fights Krishna, then gives him his daughter

whoIsWho.name: Jambavati
whoIsWho.role: Jambavan's daughter, who becomes one of Krishna's wives

whoIsWho.name: Satyabhama
whoIsWho.role: given to Krishna in marriage by her father, Satrajit, as an apology for the false accusation

/stories/syamantaka-jewel/.whyItMatters: The tale is unusual as Krishna's only true detective story, and is recited even today as a remedy for anyone falsely accused of wrongdoing.

/cosmology/cosmogony-creation-accounts/.intro: This page collects the many ways Hindu texts describe how the universe began, from the oldest Vedic hymns that admit even the gods may not know the answer, to later stories of a golden cosmic egg, a lotus growing from Vishnu's navel with Brahma seated on it, or the Goddess as the power behind every act of creation. It keeps these accounts side by side, without picking one true version.
/cosmology/cosmogony-creation-accounts/.whyItMatters: Understanding that Hindu cosmology holds multiple, sometimes contradictory creation stories together helps explain why the tradition treats scripture as a layered library of perspectives rather than a single fixed account.

/deities/kamadeva-and-minor-deities/.intro: This page introduces several important but lesser gods: Kamadeva, the god of desire who is burned to ash by Shiva and later reborn as Krishna's son Pradyumna; the divine architect Vishvakarma; the physician-god Dhanvantari; the eight elemental Vasus; and the great mother-goddesses Aditi and Diti, from whom the gods and demons descend.

whoIsWho.name: Kamadeva
whoIsWho.role: the god of love and desire, burned by Shiva and reborn as Pradyumna

whoIsWho.name: Rati
whoIsWho.role: Kamadeva's wife, who later raises her reborn husband in secret

whoIsWho.name: Aditi
whoIsWho.role: mother of the gods (devas)

whoIsWho.name: Diti
whoIsWho.role: Aditi's sister and mother of many demons (asuras)

/deities/kamadeva-and-minor-deities/.whyItMatters: These minor deities fill out the working machinery of the Hindu cosmos, standing behind everyday concerns like love, craftsmanship, healing, and the elements.

/stories/mahabharata/03-vana-parva/.intro: The Vana Parva covers the twelve years the Pandavas and Draupadi spend exiled in the forest after losing everything in the rigged dice game. Along the way they hear dozens of consoling stories from wandering sages, including the tales of Nala and Damayanti, Savitri winning her husband back from Death, and a condensed retelling of the entire Ramayana, while Arjuna leaves to win divine weapons from the gods.

whoIsWho.name: Yudhishthira
whoIsWho.role: the eldest Pandava, whose loss at dice caused the exile and who receives most of the consoling stories

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: the shared wife of the Pandavas, who endures the exile alongside her husbands

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: leaves the group to perform austerities and receive weapons from Shiva and Indra

whoIsWho.name: Bhima
whoIsWho.role: kills several demons the family encounters during the exile

/stories/mahabharata/03-vana-parva/.whyItMatters: The book is the Mahabharata's great storehouse of side-tales, using stories of other sufferers to console the Pandavas and to teach lessons about fate, duty, and endurance that echo their own situation.

/stories/characters/barbarika-khatu-shya.intro: Barbarika is a mighty archer, grandson of Bhima, who owns three magic arrows powerful enough to end any battle instantly and has vowed to always fight for whichever side is losing. Realizing this vow would make the Kurukshetra war impossible to finish, Krishna tricks him into giving up his own head as a gift, then sets the still-living head on a hilltop so it can watch the entire war unfold.

whoIsWho.name: Barbarika
whoIsWho.role: the archer whose three arrows and vow to help the losing side threaten to make the war unwinnable

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: persuades Barbarika to sacrifice his head before the war begins

whoIsWho.name: Ghatotkacha
whoIsWho.role: Barbarika's father and Bhima's son

/stories/characters/barbarika-khatu-shya.whyItMatters: Barbarika's story is not part of the standard Sanskrit Mahabharata but comes from regional and folk tradition; today he is worshipped across Rajasthan as Khatu Shyam, especially by those facing hardship or defeat.

/stories/dhruva/.intro: A young prince named Dhruva is humiliated when his stepmother tells him he has no right to sit on his father's lap, so he leaves home to win a place greater than anyone has ever held, through devotion to Vishnu. His extreme fasting and meditation eventually earns him a vision of the god, who grants him the position of the Pole Star, fixed at the center of the turning sky.

whoIsWho.name: Dhruva
whoIsWho.role: the boy whose devotion wins him the Pole Star as his eternal home

whoIsWho.name: Suruci
whoIsWho.role: the stepmother whose insult drives Dhruva to his quest

whoIsWho.name: Sunīti
whoIsWho.role: Dhruva's mother, who is later honored alongside him in the sky

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: appears to Dhruva and grants him the boon of the polar seat

whoIsWho.name: Narada
whoIsWho.role: the sage who teaches Dhruva how to worship Vishnu

/stories/dhruva/.whyItMatters: Dhruva's story explains why the Pole Star never seems to move, and makes him, alongside Prahlada, one of the two model child-devotees held up across Hindu tradition.

/stories/savitri-satyavan/.intro: Princess Savitri knowingly marries Satyavan even after a sage warns her he will die within a year, and refuses to change her mind. When Death himself comes to take her husband's soul, Savitri follows him on foot, impresses him with her wisdom, and tricks him into granting boons that can only be fulfilled if Satyavan is alive, forcing Death to bring him back to life.

whoIsWho.name: Savitri
whoIsWho.role: the princess who outwits Death to save her husband

whoIsWho.name: Satyavan
whoIsWho.role: the exiled prince Savitri marries, knowing he is fated to die young

whoIsWho.name: Yama
whoIsWho.role: the god of death, who is outmaneuvered into restoring Satyavan's life

whoIsWho.name: Narada
whoIsWho.role: the sage who foretells Satyavan's death

/stories/savitri-satyavan/.whyItMatters: The story is the model of the devoted wife in Hindu tradition and is still honored today through the Vat Savitri fast, when married women pray for their husbands' long lives.

/stories/ekalavya/.intro: Ekalavya is a low-born forest prince who teaches himself archery by practicing in front of a clay statue of the teacher Drona, who had refused to train him, and becomes even better than Drona's star pupil, Arjuna. When Drona discovers this, he demands Ekalavya's right thumb as payment for being his teacher, even though he never formally taught him, and Ekalavya cuts it off without complaint, ruining his skill forever.

whoIsWho.name: Ekalavya
whoIsWho.role: the self-taught archer who gives up his thumb out of devotion to a teacher who rejected him

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: the royal weapons teacher who demands the thumb to protect his promise that Arjuna would be unmatched

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the Pandava archer whose supremacy is threatened by Ekalavya's skill

/stories/ekalavya/.whyItMatters: The story is read two ways today, as a lesson in devotion to a teacher, and, especially in modern readings, as a story about how caste and privilege can be used to destroy a talented outsider.

/stories/characters/abhimanyu/.intro: Abhimanyu is Arjuna's sixteen-year-old son, who knows how to break into a deadly spiral battle formation but never learned how to get out. Trapped alone inside enemy lines when a Kaurava ally blocks the other Pandavas from following him, he fights off warrior after warrior until six senior fighters attack him together and break his weapons before finally killing him, an act the epic openly calls unfair.

whoIsWho.name: Abhimanyu
whoIsWho.role: the young hero who breaks into the enemy formation but cannot escape

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: Abhimanyu's father, who swears revenge after finding his son dead

whoIsWho.name: Jayadratha
whoIsWho.role: the king who seals the gap and traps Abhimanyu inside alone

whoIsWho.name: Uttara
whoIsWho.role: Abhimanyu's wife, who is pregnant with his son when he dies

/stories/characters/abhimanyu/.whyItMatters: Abhimanyu's death is treated in the epic as the war's moral low point, and it sets off the chain of revenge that shapes the rest of the fighting.

/stories/mahabharata/07-drona-parva/.intro: The Drona Parva covers days eleven through fifteen of the Kurukshetra war, fought under the second Kaurava commander, Drona. It includes some of the war's most disturbing moments: the killing of the boy warrior Abhimanyu by six men at once, Krishna faking a sunset to expose a hidden warrior so Arjuna can kill him, and Drona's own death by trickery and beheading after being falsely told his son had died.

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: the Kaurava commander for these five days, eventually killed while unarmed and grieving

whoIsWho.name: Abhimanyu
whoIsWho.role: Arjuna's young son, killed by six warriors ganging up on him

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: swears revenge for his son and kills the king who trapped him

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: engineers the tricks that bring down both Jayadratha and Drona

/stories/mahabharata/07-drona-parva/.whyItMatters: This book marks the point where both sides abandon the war's agreed rules of fair combat, and the story treats every one of these events as a serious moral failure, not a triumph.

/deities/trimurti-and-tridevi/.intro: The Trimurti is the idea that creation, preservation, and destruction are handled by three gods, Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, while the Tridevi are their three wife-goddesses, Sarasvati, Lakshmi, and Parvati. Some traditions describe the goddesses' power as what makes each god's function possible. Different schools argue that one god, or the Goddess, is the supreme being over the others, and this page lays out each claim without declaring a winner.

whoIsWho.name: Brahma
whoIsWho.role: the creator god, paired with Sarasvati

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: the preserver god, paired with Lakshmi

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: the destroyer god, paired with Parvati

whoIsWho.name: Sarasvati, Lakshmi, and Parvati
whoIsWho.role: the goddesses whose power is said, in some traditions, to make each god's role possible

/deities/trimurti-and-tridevi/.whyItMatters: Understanding the Trimurti explains why Hindu traditions can honor different gods as supreme without contradiction, since each stream reads the same three-part structure through its own lens.

/stories/shankhachuda-tulasi/.intro: Shankhachuda is a demon who becomes unbeatable in battle because of his wife Tulasi's perfect faithfulness to him. To defeat him, Vishnu disguises himself as Shankhachuda and tricks Tulasi into breaking her vow without realizing it, which allows Shiva to kill the now-unprotected demon. When Tulasi discovers the deception, she curses Vishnu, and in return he turns her into the sacred basil plant named for her, linked to his worship.

whoIsWho.name: Shankhachuda
whoIsWho.role: the demon whose invincibility depends on his wife's unbroken faithfulness

whoIsWho.name: Tulasi
whoIsWho.role: his devoted wife, tricked into breaking her vow and later transformed into the tulasi plant

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: disguises himself as the demon to break the spell, then accepts Tulasi's curse

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: strikes down Shankhachuda once his protection is gone

/stories/shankhachuda-tulasi/.whyItMatters: The story explains why the tulasi (holy basil) plant is treated as sacred to Vishnu and is paired with his worship in households across India.

/stories/yayati/.intro: King Yayati is cursed with sudden old age by his father-in-law, the sage Shukra, after secretly fathering children with his wife's servant, Sharmishtha. The curse lifts only if one of his sons trades their youth for his old age; only the youngest, Puru, agrees. A thousand years later, having learned that indulging desire only feeds it, Yayati returns Puru's youth and makes him heir instead of his older brothers.

whoIsWho.name: Yayati
whoIsWho.role: the king cursed with premature old age, who learns the futility of indulging desire

whoIsWho.name: Sukra (Shukra)
whoIsWho.role: Yayati's father-in-law, the sage who curses him

whoIsWho.name: Puru
whoIsWho.role: the youngest son who trades his youth for his father's old age and is rewarded with the throne

whoIsWho.name: Devayani
whoIsWho.role: Yayati's wife, whose father pronounces the curse after learning of his secret second family

/stories/yayati/.whyItMatters: Yayati's choice to favor Puru over his elder sons is the reason the Pandavas' own lineage descends through Puru rather than through Yadu, ancestor of Krishna's clan.

/stories/shakuntala-bharata/.intro: Shakuntala, daughter of a sage and a heavenly nymph, secretly marries King Dushyanta in the forest, on condition that their son will be his heir. Years later, when she brings their son to court, Dushyanta denies knowing her, and only a voice from the sky forces him to admit the truth. Their son, Bharata, grows up to become a legendary emperor, and India's ancient name, Bharatavarsha, comes from him.

whoIsWho.name: Shakuntala
whoIsWho.role: the forest-raised woman who marries a king and is later publicly rejected by him

whoIsWho.name: Dushyanta
whoIsWho.role: the king who denies his marriage to Shakuntala until a divine voice corrects him

whoIsWho.name: Bharata
whoIsWho.role: their son, who becomes a great emperor and gives his name to the land

whoIsWho.name: Kanva
whoIsWho.role: the sage who raises Shakuntala after she is abandoned as an infant

/stories/shakuntala-bharata/.whyItMatters: This story, later famously reworked into a play by the poet Kalidasa, is the origin story for the name "Bharat," still used today as India's official name.

/stories/characters/ashvatthama/.intro: Ashvatthama is Drona's only son, born with a magic gem in his forehead that makes him nearly invincible. Enraged that his father was tricked into laying down his weapons and beheaded, he sneaks into the enemy camp at night and kills the sleeping soldiers, among them Draupadi's five sons. Krishna curses him to wander the earth for three thousand years, unable to die, for striking at an unborn child too.

whoIsWho.name: Ashvatthama
whoIsWho.role: Drona's son, cursed to endless wandering for the night massacre

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: his father, tricked into laying down his weapons and then killed

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: pronounces the curse that condemns Ashvatthama to immortality as punishment

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: demands vengeance and the gem from Ashvatthama's forehead after her sons are killed in their sleep

/stories/characters/ashvatthama/.whyItMatters: Ashvatthama is counted among a small group of beings said to be still alive today, making him one of Hindu tradition's most vivid images of guilt that can never be erased.

/stories/mahabharata/10-sauptika-parva/.intro: The Sauptika Parva describes the night after the eighteen-day war ends, when the last three surviving Kaurava warriors sneak into the sleeping enemy camp for revenge. Ashvatthama kills the man who beheaded his father and the five sons of Draupadi, while his companions set the camp on fire and cut down anyone who flees, turning a war the Pandavas had already won into a massacre of the unarmed and asleep.

whoIsWho.name: Ashvatthama
whoIsWho.role: leads the night raid and kills Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi's five sons in their sleep

whoIsWho.name: Kripa and Kritavarma
whoIsWho.role: the two surviving allies who guard the camp gates and set it ablaze

whoIsWho.name: Dhrishtadyumna
whoIsWho.role: Drona's killer, murdered in his sleep in revenge

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: demands justice after learning her sons were killed while helpless

/stories/mahabharata/10-sauptika-parva/.whyItMatters: The book is the Mahabharata's clearest statement that even a just war can end in an atrocity, since the massacre happens only after the war is effectively already decided.

/deities/surya-and-his-family/.intro: Surya is the sun god, whose radiance is so intense that his wife cannot bear to be near him, so she leaves a shadow double in her place and flees in the form of a mare. Their children include Yama, judge of the dead, the river goddess Yamuna, the healer twins the Ashvins, and Manu, ancestor of humanity. The shadow wife bears more children, including the planet-god Shani.

whoIsWho.name: Surya
whoIsWho.role: the sun god at the center of a large divine family

whoIsWho.name: Sanjna (Saranyu)
whoIsWho.role: Surya's true wife, who cannot bear his heat and secretly leaves

whoIsWho.name: Chhaya
whoIsWho.role: the shadow double Sanjna leaves behind to take her place

whoIsWho.name: Yama
whoIsWho.role: Surya's son, the first being to die and the judge of the dead

whoIsWho.name: Manu
whoIsWho.role: Surya's son, considered the ancestor of the current human race

/deities/surya-and-his-family/.whyItMatters: Surya's household explains the origins of death, the calendar, the Ashvin healer-gods, and the astrological planet Shani, tying the sun to nearly every corner of the wider cosmology.

/stories/mahabharata/02-sabha-parva/.intro: The Sabha Parva tells how Yudhishthira rises to the height of his power, crowned emperor after a grand sacrifice, and then loses everything in a single rigged dice game. His cousin Duryodhana's uncle cheats him out of his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and finally his wife Draupadi, who is dragged into the hall and nearly stripped in public before elders too paralyzed by the question of law to stop it.

whoIsWho.name: Yudhishthira
whoIsWho.role: the Pandava king whose gambling addiction loses everything, including his wife

whoIsWho.name: Duryodhana
whoIsWho.role: the rival cousin who arranges the dice game to destroy the Pandavas

whoIsWho.name: Shakuni
whoIsWho.role: Duryodhana's uncle, who cheats at every throw

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: staked and nearly stripped after being dragged into the assembly

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: kills the insulting king Shishupala earlier in the same book, at the height of Yudhishthira's power

/stories/mahabharata/02-sabha-parva/.whyItMatters: The dice game and Draupadi's humiliation in this book are named again and again later in the epic as the true cause of the war, more than any battlefield grievance.

/stories/bhagavad-gita/07-to-12-bhakti-s.intro: This page covers chapters seven through twelve of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna explains his divine nature, describes himself as the greatest example within every category of creation, and grants Arjuna a terrifying vision of his cosmic form, containing every world and the war's coming deaths. The section ends by teaching that loving devotion, open to people of any background, is an easier path to God than pure knowledge.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the speaker of these chapters, who reveals his cosmic form to Arjuna

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: asks to see Krishna's true form and reacts with terror and awe

/stories/bhagavad-gita/07-to-12-bhakti-s.whyItMatters: This section contains the Gita's most quoted line, "I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds," and its clearest statement that sincere devotion, not birth or learning, is what reaches God.

/places/vaishno-devi-trikuta-katra/.intro: Vaishno Devi is a cave shrine in the Trikuta hills above Katra, where the Goddess is worshipped not as a statue but as three natural rock formations. According to the shrine's legend, she flees up the mountain from a tantric who pursues her, and beheads him at the cave's mouth; out of mercy she grants him a boon, so no pilgrimage to her is complete without visiting his shrine nearby.

whoIsWho.name: Vaishno Devi
whoIsWho.role: the goddess worshipped in the cave as three natural rock forms

whoIsWho.name: Bhairavnath
whoIsWho.role: the pursuer she beheads, whom she then forgives and blesses

whoIsWho.name: Shridhar
whoIsWho.role: the poor devotee whose feast first reveals the goddess's miraculous nature

/places/vaishno-devi-trikuta-katra/.whyItMatters: Vaishno Devi is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in India, drawing millions of devotees each year to a shrine built entirely around natural rock rather than carved images.

/places/arupadai-veedu-murugan/.intro: The Arupadai Veedu are six sacred sites across Tamil Nadu, each tied to one chapter of the war-god Murugan's life story: his birth and battle against the demon Surapadman, his marriage to the warrior-bride Devasena, his time as a renouncing ascetic, the moment he teaches his own father Shiva the meaning of the sacred syllable Om, and his marriage to the tribal girl Valli.

whoIsWho.name: Murugan (also called Skanda or Kartikeya)
whoIsWho.role: the six-faced war god honored across all six shrines

whoIsWho.name: Surapadman
whoIsWho.role: the demon Murugan defeats in battle, whose body becomes his peacock mount and rooster banner

whoIsWho.name: Devasena
whoIsWho.role: Murugan's first wife, given to him by the gods after his victory

whoIsWho.name: Valli
whoIsWho.role: a hunter's daughter Murugan woos and marries in the hills, his second, more human romance

/places/arupadai-veedu-murugan/.whyItMatters: Visiting all six shrines in order is treated as tracing the whole arc of Murugan's life, from warrior to bridegroom to teacher to graceful protector of the land.

/stories/characters/ghatotkacha/.intro: Ghatotkacha is the rakshasa son of Bhima, born and grown to full size and strength within a single day, gifted with illusion-warfare that lets him fight from the sky. During a night battle, he wreaks havoc on the Kaurava army until their leaders beg Karna to use his one-time weapon on him rather than save it for Arjuna — and Krishna celebrates the boy's death, since it keeps Arjuna safe.

whoIsWho.name: Ghatotkacha
whoIsWho.role: Bhima's demon son, whose death in battle secretly saves Arjuna's life

whoIsWho.name: Bhima

/stories/characters/ghatotkacha/.whyItMatters: Ghatotkacha's death is framed as a hidden turning point of the war, a sacrifice that saves the hero Arjuna without either side realizing it at the time.

/stories/mahabharata/08-karna-parva/.intro: The Karna Parva covers the last two days Karna commands the Kaurava army, after Drona's death. Weighed down by three separate curses working against him at once, Karna finally duels Arjuna and, at the crucial moment, his chariot wheel sinks into the earth and he forgets the mantra for his most powerful weapon, leaving him helpless when Arjuna beheads him.

whoIsWho.name: Karna
whoIsWho.role: the tragic hero who commands the army for two days before dying in his final duel with Arjuna

whoIsWho.name: Krishna

/stories/mahabharata/08-karna-parva/.whyItMatters: Karna's death is treated as the war's true turning point, since with him gone the Kaurava army has no warrior left who can match Arjuna.

/stories/rukmini-harana/.intro: Princess Rukmini secretly writes to Krishna, whom she has never met but loves by reputation, begging him to carry her off before her brother can force her to marry his ally Shishupala. Krishna races to her city, snatches her from a temple procession in front of the assembled kings, and marries her, later sparing her brother's life at her request even after defeating him in battle.

/stories/rukmini-harana/.whyItMatters: The story shows Krishna's central marriage as a rescue the bride herself designs and requests, which is why it is celebrated in temples across South India as a model wedding.

/places/jagannath-puri-purushottama-kshe.intro: Jagannath Puri is a major pilgrimage city on the Odisha coast where Krishna is worshipped in an unusual form: a plain wooden log with round eyes and no arms, alongside his brother and sister. According to legend, a divine carpenter began carving the images behind locked doors but was interrupted before finishing, which is why the statues remain deliberately unfinished to this day.

/places/jagannath-puri-purushottama-kshe.whyItMatters: Puri is the site of the Ratha Yatra, the festival that gave English the word "juggernaut," when the three deities are pulled through the streets in giant chariots.

/stories/indradyumna-akupara-oldest-bein.intro: A king named Indradyumna falls from heaven because no one remembers him anymore, and he is told he can return only if he finds someone who does. He is sent from the sage Markandeya to an owl, then a crane, and at last to a tortoise named Akupara, who recognizes him — because the lake he lives in was dug out by the hooves of cattle Indradyumna gave away.

whoIsWho.role: the fallen king searching for someone who still remembers his good deeds

whoIsWho.name: Akupara
whoIsWho.role: the ancient tortoise who finally recognizes the king through the mark his generosity left on the land

/stories/indradyumna-akupara-oldest-bein.whyItMatters: The story teaches that a person's good deeds can outlast even their name being remembered, since it is the changed landscape, not the memory of the king himself, that finally proves who he was.

/cosmology/.intro: This section explains how Hindu tradition understands time itself: not as a straight line from a beginning to an end, but as an endless cycle of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, playing out in units that range from the blink of an eye to spans of hundreds of trillions of years. Start here to understand the "cosmic address" used throughout the rest of the site to place every story and era.
/cosmology/.whyItMatters: Every date and era used elsewhere on this site is really a position within these cycles, so this section is the key to understanding how Hindu tradition places any given event in time.

/manvantaras/.intro: This section tracks the fourteen great cosmic ages, called Manvantaras, that make up one full day in the life of the god Brahma. Each Manvantara has its own presiding ancestor of humanity (a Manu), its own king of the gods, and its own set of seven sages. We are currently living in the seventh of these fourteen ages.
/manvantaras/.whyItMatters: Use this section to see where the Puranic king lists, floods, and avatar stories fit inside the wider cosmic calendar, and to find the current age from which every other dated story on this site is measured.

/deities/.intro: This section is the who's-who of Hindu gods and cosmic beings, organized not by time period but by identity, since the same deities reappear across every age. It covers the three-part godhead of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva; their ten and more avatars; the Goddess in her many forms; and the wider worlds of gods and demons.
/deities/.whyItMatters: Come here when a story mentions a god you don't recognize, or when you want to see how the same deity's different names and forms connect across the whole site.

/lineages/.intro: This section traces the royal family trees that run through the timeline's stories, mostly descending from two dynasties founded by the children of Manu: the solar line that leads to Rama, and the lunar line that leads to the Pandavas and Krishna. Since these families span many different ages, their stories are gathered here rather than scattered across each era.
/lineages/.whyItMatters: Use this section to see how kings and heroes from different stories are actually related, and how a single family's choices generations earlier echo forward into the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.

/stories/.intro: This section holds full-length treatments of the biggest individual episodes in Hindu tradition, from the two great epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, told book by book, to standalone tales like the churning of the ocean and the whole life of Krishna. These are the stories too large to fit inside a single page about their time period.
/stories/.whyItMatters: This is the place to go for the complete version of any story mentioned briefly elsewhere on the site, since each entry gathers every named character, variant telling, and source in one place.

/dharma/.intro: This section explains the ideas behind the stories: concepts like dharma (duty and cosmic order), karma and rebirth, the four goals of life, the stages of life, and the different schools of Hindu philosophy. These are the recurring principles that motivate characters' choices throughout the timeline's narratives.
/dharma/.whyItMatters: Come here when a story references an idea like karma, moksha, or varna and you want the concept explained on its own terms, apart from any single character's story.

/places/.intro: This section maps the sacred landscape of India: rivers, mountains, temple cities, and whole pilgrimage circuits where, according to tradition, a story from the timeline actually touched the earth. Each entry explains the local legend that explains why a particular site became holy.
/places/.whyItMatters: Use this section to see where a story you've read elsewhere is still marked on the map today, and which pilgrimage traditions grew out of it.

/teachers/.intro: This section covers the historical teachers, poet-saints, and religious orders that carried Hindu practice forward through the centuries: philosophers like Shankara, devotional poets like Mirabai and Tulsidas, and the different sects built around Vishnu, Shiva, and the Goddess. Unlike most of this site, these are figures whose dates can often be checked against outside historical records.
/teachers/.whyItMatters: Come here to see who actually built the schools of thought and worship practiced today, and how they trace their authority back to the older scriptures and stories told elsewhere on this site.

/beings/.intro: This section catalogs the many kinds of beings that exist between gods and humans: celestial musicians, tree-spirits, serpent-people, demon races, ghosts, and the named magical animals of the epics, like the eagle Garuda and the wish-granting cow Kamadhenu. None of these classes are simply good or evil; the same family of beings can include both villains and devoted heroes.
/beings/.whyItMatters: Use this section to understand a creature's place in the wider cosmic order whenever a story mentions it without much explanation.

/symbols/.intro: This section catalogs the objects, weapons, symbols, and traditional arts that appear throughout Hindu stories: named weapons like Vishnu's discus and Arjuna's bow, sacred symbols like Om and the lotus, the animals the gods ride, and the sixty-four traditional arts a well-rounded person was expected to master.
/symbols/.whyItMatters: Come here whenever a story mentions an object or symbol by name and you want to know its origin, its usual owner, and what it stands for.

/texts/.intro: This section explains the scriptures themselves: the difference between the Vedas, treated as eternally revealed, and the later texts like the epics and the eighteen Puranas, which are composed but still highly authoritative. It sorts out which text says what, how each was traditionally dated versus how scholars date it today, and which texts are the real sources behind the stories told elsewhere on the site.
/texts/.whyItMatters: Use this section whenever you want to know how reliable or how old a claim is, since every event elsewhere on the site should trace back to a specific text cataloged here.

/.intro: This is the master index for a project that maps the entire Hindu understanding of time, from the smallest fraction of a second to the 311-trillion-year life of the god Brahma, and places every story, king, and text at its own address on that scale. It works forward from cosmic ages down to individual epics, gods, family trees, sacred places, and the scriptures that record them all.
/.whyItMatters: This page is the front door to the whole site; start here to find your way to any section, whether you want the cosmic calendar, a specific god, a royal lineage, or one particular story.

/lineages/suryavamsha-and-chandravamsha/.intro: This page traces the two royal family trees that produce almost every major hero in Hindu epic literature: the Solar dynasty, descending through King Ikshvaku to Rama, and the Lunar dynasty, descending through King Yayati's son Puru to the Pandavas, and through his other son Yadu to Krishna. Both families descend from the same ancestor, Manu, the survivor of the great flood.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: born into the Lunar dynasty's Yadava branch

/lineages/suryavamsha-and-chandravamsha/.whyItMatters: Nearly every named king and hero elsewhere on this site belongs to one of these two families, so this page is the key to seeing how far-flung characters are actually related.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.intro: This page describes what Hindu scripture predicts about the current age, Kali Yuga, the last and worst of the four ages, when virtue is reduced to a quarter of its original strength. The texts describe a long decline in honesty, health, and justice, followed eventually by the arrival of Kalki, a final avatar of Vishnu who will end the age's corruption and restart the cycle with a new golden age.

whoIsWho.name: Kalki
whoIsWho.role: the future avatar of Vishnu who will appear at the end of Kali Yuga riding a white horse

whoIsWho.name: Vishnuyasha
whoIsWho.role: Kalki's father, a brahmin in the village of Shambhala, according to the prophecy

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.whyItMatters: This page explains why Hindu tradition considers the present era to be one of moral decline, and gives the traditional endpoint, still hundreds of thousands of years away, when that decline is expected to reverse.

/deities/shiva-myth-cycle/.intro: This page collects the major stories of Shiva: how he burns the demon of desire to ash, catches the falling river Ganga in his hair, drinks a world-poison that turns his throat blue, destroys three flying demon cities with a single arrow, and dances the cosmic dance that both destroys and renews the universe. These stories present Shiva as the highest reality, with the other gods shown as his instruments.

whoIsWho.role: the god at the center of every story on this page

whoIsWho.name: Parvati
whoIsWho.role: Shiva's wife, present in several of the stories including the burning of Kama and the swallowing of poison

whoIsWho.name: Kama
whoIsWho.role: the love god, burned to ash by Shiva's third eye

whoIsWho.name: Ganga
whoIsWho.role: the river goddess whose fall to earth is broken by Shiva's hair

/deities/shiva-myth-cycle/.whyItMatters: The page is written from a Shaiva point of view, meaning it consistently treats Shiva, not Brahma or Vishnu, as the ultimate power behind the universe.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.intro: The Dvapara Yuga is the third of the four cosmic ages, when virtue and vice are evenly balanced. It is the age of Krishna, the Mahabharata war, and the sage Vyasa, who organized the Vedas and composed the great epic this age is remembered for. The age ends with Krishna's death and the sinking of his city, Dwarka, which traditionally begins the present age, Kali Yuga.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: the central figure of this age, whose life and death frame its close

whoIsWho.name: Vyasa
whoIsWho.role: the sage credited with organizing the Vedas and composing the Mahabharata during this age

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
whoIsWho.role: the warrior Krishna guides through the Bhagavad Gita during the war that defines this era

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.whyItMatters: This page is the cosmic-calendar anchor for the entire Mahabharata story world, showing exactly where Krishna's life and the great war sit on the larger timeline of ages.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/.intro: This page covers the seventh of fourteen great cosmic ages, the one we are currently living in, presided over by the ancestor-figure Manu, who survives a world-ending flood at its start by following the warning of a fish that is really Vishnu in disguise. All of recorded Hindu history, the two great epics, and the well-known avatars of Vishnu take place within this single age.

whoIsWho.name: Manu (Vaivasvata)
whoIsWho.role: the ancestor of humanity for this age, who survives the flood that opens it

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: takes the form of a fish, Matsya, to warn and save Manu

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/.whyItMatters: This page is the frame that holds the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and every well-known avatar story, since all of them are said to happen within this one cosmic age.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.intro: The Treta Yuga is the second of the four cosmic ages, when virtue has dropped to three-quarters strength and grand ritual sacrifice becomes the main way people uphold order. It is the age of three of Vishnu's avatars: the dwarf Vamana who tricks a generous demon-king, the axe-wielding priest-warrior Parashurama, and Rama, whose story, the Ramayana, defines the age.

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: the central figure of this age, prince of Ayodhya and hero of the Ramayana

whoIsWho.name: Vamana
whoIsWho.role: an earlier avatar of Vishnu in this age, the dwarf who outwits the demon-king Bali

whoIsWho.name: Parashurama
whoIsWho.role: another avatar of this age, the warrior-priest who wipes out corrupt kings

whoIsWho.name: Sita
whoIsWho.role: Rama's wife, whose abduction sets the Ramayana's plot in motion

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.whyItMatters: This page places Rama's life on the larger timeline of ages, right after Vishnu's earlier appearances in the same era as Vamana and Parashurama.

/stories/ramayana/.intro: This is the overview page for the Ramayana, one of Hindu tradition's two great epics, telling the life of Prince Rama of Ayodhya across seven books: his birth, his exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, the war to rescue her, and his eventual return home as king. Countless retellings of this story exist across Asia in different languages and religions.

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: the exiled prince of Ayodhya whose story the epic follows

whoIsWho.name: Sita
whoIsWho.role: Rama's wife, abducted by Ravana, at the center of the plot

whoIsWho.name: Ravana
whoIsWho.role: the ten-headed demon king of Lanka who abducts Sita

whoIsWho.name: Hanuman
whoIsWho.role: the devoted monkey-warrior who finds Sita and helps win the war

whoIsWho.name: Lakshmana
whoIsWho.role: Rama's loyal brother, who accompanies him through exile and war

/stories/ramayana/.whyItMatters: This page is the entry point to the epic's seven books, and explains how the version most people know differs from the older core text and from the many other Ramayanas told in other Indian languages, and in Jain, Buddhist, and Southeast Asian traditions.

/deities/devas-asuras-and-the-lokas/.intro: This page maps the vertical structure of the Hindu universe: fourteen worlds stacked above and below the earth, home to gods, sages, and serpent-people in the upper and lower realms. It introduces the devas (gods) and asuras (their demon rivals), explaining that both groups are half-brothers, children of the same father by two different mothers, which makes their conflict a family struggle rather than a battle between good and evil.

whoIsWho.name: Indra
whoIsWho.role: king of the gods and ruler of heaven, whose throne is repeatedly threatened by demons and ascetics

whoIsWho.name: Kashyapa
whoIsWho.role: the father of both the gods and many demon lineages, through different wives

whoIsWho.name: Prahlada and Bali
whoIsWho.role: devout demon-kings who show that not every asura is a villain

whoIsWho.name: Ravana and Hiranyakashipu
whoIsWho.role: demon kings whose tyranny is ended by different forms of Vishnu

/deities/devas-asuras-and-the-lokas/.whyItMatters: Use this page to understand the cosmic geography and the family relationships behind every deva-versus-asura story told elsewhere on the site.

/stories/characters/.intro: This section holds dedicated pages for the individual characters of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata who have enough of their own story, across multiple books and later retellings, to deserve a page of their own rather than just appearing inside the main narrative. It covers everyone from the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi to Rama's allies and enemies in the Ramayana.
/stories/characters/.whyItMatters: Come here when you want the complete picture of one character's arc pulled together from across an epic's many books, rather than scattered pieces from each chapter.

/texts/smriti-puranas/.intro: This page introduces the Puranas, the large body of scripture that tells most of the stories used throughout this site: how the world was created, the ages of the fourteen ancestor-figures called Manus, the deeds of the avatars, and the family trees of ancient kings. Tradition counts eighteen major Puranas and eighteen lesser ones, all credited to the sage Vyasa, though which text belongs on which list is disputed.
/texts/smriti-puranas/.whyItMatters: This page is the map to which scripture says what, since almost every story elsewhere on the site traces back to one specific Purana named here.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.intro: This page covers the 28th of the seventy-one great four-age cycles that make up our current cosmic era, the one containing nearly every story and figure this site records. Within it, the golden Satya age, the ritual-centered Treta age, and the balanced Dvapara age have already passed; we are living in its fourth and final quarter, the declining Kali age.
/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.whyItMatters: This page is the direct parent of the four yuga pages, showing how the ages of Rama, Krishna, and the present day all sit inside this one specific cycle rather than some other one of the seventy-one.

/stories/mahabharata/.intro: This is the overview page for the Mahabharata, the longer of Hindu tradition's two great epics, telling the story of a war between two branches of one royal family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, across eighteen books. It also contains the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to the warrior Arjuna on the battlefield, and is traditionally said to hold every story that matters, since it calls itself the fifth Veda.

/stories/mahabharata/.whyItMatters: This page is the entry point to the epic's eighteen books, and explains how the version most people know grew, over centuries, from a shorter core into the longest poem in the world.

/texts/shruti-vedas-and-upanishads/.intro: This page explains the Vedas, the oldest and most authoritative layer of Hindu scripture, believed to be eternally revealed truth rather than something a human being wrote. It covers the four Vedas, their different layers of hymn, ritual instruction, and philosophy, and the Upanishads, the philosophical writings at the end of each Veda that ask what the self and ultimate reality really are.
/texts/shruti-vedas-and-upanishads/.whyItMatters: This page explains why the Vedas outrank every other Hindu text in authority, and gives the philosophical foundation, especially the Upanishads, that later texts like the Bhagavad Gita build on.

/texts/smriti-itihasa-epics/.intro: This page covers Itihasa, meaning "thus it was," the category that holds Hindu tradition's two great epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Unlike the Vedas, these are considered human-composed rather than eternally revealed, though they carry enormous authority and are treated as genuine, if ancient, history.
/texts/smriti-itihasa-epics/.whyItMatters: This page is the map to how the two epics are structured, how many different versions of each exist across India and Asia, and how scholars date them differently from how tradition dates them.

/dharma/purusharthas-and-karma-samsara-m.intro: This page explains two of Hindu thought's central ideas: the four proper aims of a human life (duty, wealth, pleasure, and liberation), and the engine of karma, rebirth, and release that carries a soul through many lifetimes. Different schools of thought rank these aims differently and disagree about what liberation actually means, and the page lays out each position without picking a winner.
/dharma/purusharthas-and-karma-samsara-m.whyItMatters: This page explains the underlying logic of reward, rebirth, and liberation that quietly shapes the motivations of nearly every character across the site's stories.

/texts/bhagavata-purana-skandha-map/.intro: This page maps the twelve books of the Bhagavata Purana, the scripture most responsible for the popular image of Krishna, book by book. Its longest and most famous book, the tenth, tells Krishna's entire life story, from his birth in a prison cell to his years as a cowherd boy to his rule as a king in Dwarka.

/texts/bhagavata-purana-skandha-map/.whyItMatters: This page helps locate any Krishna story elsewhere on the site within its proper book and chapter of this single, enormously influential scripture.

/stories/bhagavad-gita/.intro: This is the hub page for the Bhagavad Gita, the eighteen-chapter conversation between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, spoken on the battlefield just before the Mahabharata war begins. Arjuna, refusing to fight his own relatives, is taught by Krishna about duty, the eternal soul, devotion, and the nature of God, in what became the most widely read philosophical text in Hindu tradition.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: Arjuna's charioteer and teacher throughout the conversation, revealed as God himself

whoIsWho.name: Arjuna
