/stories/bhagavad-gita/.whyItMatters: This page links out to a deep dive on all eighteen chapters, and explains why a battlefield speech became one of the most commented-on religious texts in the world, studied by wildly different schools of thought that each read it as confirming their own view.

/stories/vishwamitra-vasishtha/.intro: This page tells the long rivalry between Vishwamitra, a king who wants to become a sage of the highest rank through sheer willpower, and Vasishtha, a sage born into that rank who refuses to simply hand it over. Across many lifetimes of effort, Vishwamitra suffers repeated setbacks driven by his own anger, until he finally masters it, and Vasishtha freely gives him the title he could never take by force.

/stories/vishwamitra-vasishtha/.whyItMatters: The rivalry is Hindu tradition's central story about whether spiritual rank can be earned rather than only inherited by birth, and its answer is that it can, but only once anger itself has been conquered.

/places/sthala-puranas-major-temples/.intro: This page collects the origin legends of major Hindu temples that are not covered by the more famous lists like the twelve Jyotirlingas or the fifty-one Shakti Peethas. Each temple has its own story explaining how a particular god chose that exact spot, such as Krishna's image floating ashore as a sacred log at Puri, or Shiva being unable to lift a sacred stone he had given away at Gokarna.
/places/sthala-puranas-major-temples/.whyItMatters: Use this page when a story elsewhere on the site mentions why a specific temple exists, since it collects the local legend behind places like Tirupati, Puri, Pandharpur, and Rameswaram in one place.

/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.intro: This page lines up two different clocks for the same stretch of time: the traditional dating used in Hindu scripture, where the present age began in 3102 BCE, and the mainstream historical dating used by archaeologists and scholars, which sees the same story unfold much later. It runs from the Indus Valley civilization up through modern reform movements, flagging every point where the two clocks disagree.
/manvantaras/manvantara-07-vaivasvata/ma.whyItMatters: This page shows how far apart Hindu tradition's own timeline and modern scholarly history really are, and exactly where the two accounts pull apart.

/stories/ramayana/1-bala-kanda/.intro: This is the first book of the Ramayana, covering Rama's birth as an answer to his father's prayer for sons, his boyhood training under the sage Vishwamitra, his killing of the demon Tataka, and his marriage to Sita after he alone can string and break the bow of Shiva. It closes with the warrior-sage Parashurama testing him and recognizing him as Vishnu.

whoIsWho.role: the sage who takes the boy Rama from his father to guard his sacrifice from demons

whoIsWho.name: Parashurama
whoIsWho.role: an earlier warrior form of Vishnu, furious that Rama has broken Shiva's bow, who yields his own power to him

/stories/ramayana/1-bala-kanda/.whyItMatters: This book sets up nearly everything the rest of the epic depends on: Rama's divine identity, his marriage to Sita, and the family ties that will shape the exile to come.

/places/12-jyotirlingas/.intro: This page catalogs the twelve Jyotirlingas, the most sacred shrines of Shiva, each said to mark a spot where he appeared as an infinite pillar of fire to settle a dispute between Brahma and Vishnu over which of them was supreme. Scripture describes sixty-four such sites in total, but only these twelve are treated as supreme across all of India.
/places/12-jyotirlingas/.whyItMatters: This page gives the story behind each of the twelve shrines, including several whose exact location is still disputed between rival towns today.

/deities/saptarishi/.intro: The Saptarishi are the seven greatest sages of Hindu tradition, a role that is refilled with new people at the start of each of the fourteen great cosmic ages. Different scriptures name the seven differently, but they are always credited with preserving the Vedas, fathering the priestly family lines, and standing as a council of wisdom alongside the ruling Manu of their age.

whoIsWho.name: Vasishtha
whoIsWho.role: the priest of the solar dynasty kings including Rama, and one side of the seven sages' most famous rivalry

whoIsWho.name: Vishwamitra
whoIsWho.role: a king who wins his way into the seven sages' rank through relentless self-discipline

whoIsWho.name: Agastya
whoIsWho.role: a sage sometimes counted among the seven, said to have drunk the entire ocean in one gulp

whoIsWho.name: Kashyapa
whoIsWho.role: father of the gods, demons, and many other beings, through his many wives

whoIsWho.name: Bhrigu
whoIsWho.role: a sage sometimes counted among the seven, who once kicked the sleeping Vishnu to test his patience

/deities/saptarishi/.whyItMatters: This page explains why one sage's name can appear on different lists across the tradition, and gathers the best-known stories of each of the seven sages in one place.

/stories/ramayana/6-yuddha-kanda/.intro: This is the sixth book of the Ramayana, covering the building of a bridge to Lanka, the long siege of the city, and the deaths of Ravana's brother Kumbhakarna, his son Indrajit, and finally Ravana himself. It ends with Sita proving her purity by fire and the couple's triumphant return to Ayodhya, where Rama is crowned king.

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: leads the war to rescue Sita and kills Ravana with a weapon given to him by the sage Agastya

whoIsWho.name: Ravana
whoIsWho.role: the ten-headed king of Lanka, killed by Rama after a fierce battle

whoIsWho.name: Hanuman
whoIsWho.role: carries Rama on his shoulders in battle and later flies off to fetch a whole mountain of healing herbs

whoIsWho.name: Lakshmana
whoIsWho.role: Rama's brother, badly wounded twice in the war and healed both times

whoIsWho.name: Vibhishana
whoIsWho.role: Ravana's own brother, who defects to Rama's side and is later crowned king of Lanka

/stories/ramayana/6-yuddha-kanda/.whyItMatters: This book is the climax of the entire epic, and the source of the famous line where Rama insists, "I think of myself as a man," even as the gods declare he is God returned to earth.

/stories/ramayana/7-uttara-kanda/.intro: This final book of the Ramayana is widely considered a later addition by scholars, and it covers events both before and after the war: Ravana's family history, Rama's banishment of the pregnant Sita over public gossip, the birth of their twin sons, and Rama's own departure from the world by walking into the river Sarayu. Many of its harshest episodes are debated as later, non-original material.

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: now king of Ayodhya, who banishes the pregnant Sita over rumors and later kills a low-born ascetic for practicing forbidden penance

whoIsWho.name: Sita
whoIsWho.role: banished to the forest while pregnant, who chooses to return to the earth rather than prove her purity a second time

whoIsWho.name: Lava and Kusha
whoIsWho.role: Rama and Sita's twin sons, raised by the sage Valmiki, who unknowingly recite their own father's life story back to him

whoIsWho.name: Valmiki
whoIsWho.role: the sage credited with composing the Ramayana, who shelters Sita and raises her sons

whoIsWho.name: Ravana
whoIsWho.role: Rama's old enemy, whose whole family history and rise to power is told in flashback at the start of this book

/stories/ramayana/7-uttara-kanda/.whyItMatters: This is the epic's most controversial book, containing both the beloved reunion of Rama with his sons and episodes, like Sita's banishment, that many readers and scholars find hard to reconcile with Rama's own character.

/places/temple-networks-and-circuits/.intro: This page catalogs the great numbered pilgrimage circuits of Hindu temples, fixed sets like the 108 Vishnu shrines sung by Tamil poet-saints called the Alvars, or the eight self-made Ganesha shrines of Maharashtra, that are meant to be visited together as one complete journey. Unlike a single holy site, a circuit isn't finished until every temple on the list has been visited.
/places/temple-networks-and-circuits/.whyItMatters: Use this page when a story elsewhere mentions a temple as part of a numbered set, since it explains which larger circuit that temple belongs to and why the number itself is treated as sacred.

/places/sapta-puri-and-sacred-cities/.intro: This page lists the seven cities and the seven rivers that Hindu tradition holds to be so sacred that dying in one of the cities, or bathing in one of the rivers, grants liberation. The seven cities include Ayodhya, where Rama was born, and Dwarka, the sea capital Krishna built and which later sank beneath the waves.
/places/sapta-puri-and-sacred-cities/.whyItMatters: This page is the map to the seven mokṣa-cities and seven sacred rivers named in every ritual bath, showing which deity, era, and story each one is tied to.

/beings/nagas-and-serpents/.intro: Nagas are a race of half-human, half-serpent beings who live in a jeweled underground realm, guard treasure and water, and are locked in an old blood feud with the great eagle Garuda. Born as the thousand sons of the sage Kashyapa, they include kings like Vasuki and Takshaka, the river-serpent Kaliya tamed by Krishna, and the goddess Manasa, who protects against snakebite.

whoIsWho.name: Vasuki
whoIsWho.role: king of the serpent people, who serves as the churning-rope when gods and demons churn the ocean for the drink of immortality

whoIsWho.name: Kaliya
whoIsWho.role: a poisonous, hundred-hooded serpent that poisons a river until the young Krishna dances on his hoods and drives him away

whoIsWho.name: Shesha (Ananta)
whoIsWho.role: the endless, thousand-hooded serpent who holds up the earth and forms the couch on which Vishnu reclines

whoIsWho.name: Takshaka
whoIsWho.role: the serpent whose bite kills a king, setting off a vow to destroy the entire serpent race

whoIsWho.name: Manasa
whoIsWho.role: the goddess of snakes, sister of Vasuki, worshipped especially in Bengal to protect against snakebite

/beings/nagas-and-serpents/.whyItMatters: This page collects the named serpent-kings and serpent-stories that appear scattered across the epics, from the ocean-churning rope Vasuki to the Kaliya Krishna dances on top of, in one place.

/places/51-shakti-peethas/.intro: This page catalogs the Shakti Peethas, shrines marking the spots where pieces of the goddess Sati's body fell to earth after she gave up her life at her father's sacrifice and a grieving Shiva carried her corpse across the world. The exact number is one of the most disputed counts in Hindu sacred geography, with different scriptures naming four, eighteen, fifty-one, or a hundred and eight shrines.

whoIsWho.name: Sati
whoIsWho.role: the goddess whose body, destroyed by her own grief and anger, falls to earth piece by piece and creates the shrines

whoIsWho.name: Shiva
whoIsWho.role: Sati's husband, whose mad grief at carrying her corpse across the world threatens to unbalance all creation

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: cuts Sati's body apart with his discus as Shiva carries it, to end his grief and restore order

whoIsWho.name: Daksha
whoIsWho.role: Sati's father, whose sacrifice she attends uninvited and where she is publicly humiliated

/places/51-shakti-peethas/.whyItMatters: This page explains why the count of these shrines differs so much between texts, and gathers the origin story, presiding goddess, and guardian god paired at each of the best-known sites.

/manvantaras/manvantara-01-svayambhuva/.intro: This is the very first of the fourteen great ages, called Manvantaras, that make up one day in the life of the god Brahma, and it is the age with the most stories attached to it. It opens just after Vishnu's Boar form lifts the earth out of the cosmic ocean. The first man and woman, Manu and Shatarupa, are born here, and their children start the earliest royal families. Two of the tradition's best-loved stories happen in this age: a boy named Dhruva becomes the pole star, and a king named Prithu milks the earth like a cow to bring out food for everyone.

whoIsWho.name: Svayambhuva Manu
whoIsWho.role: the first man, mind-born son of Brahma

whoIsWho.name: Shatarupa
whoIsWho.role: the first woman, wife of Svayambhuva Manu

whoIsWho.name: Dhruva
whoIsWho.role: a boy who wins a place in the sky as the pole star

whoIsWho.name: Prithu
whoIsWho.role: a king who "milks" the earth to bring out grain

/manvantaras/manvantara-01-svayambhuva/.whyItMatters: This age sets up humanity's first family tree and gives two of the most loved teaching stories in the tradition — Dhruva's patience and Prithu's care for the earth.

/manvantaras/manvantara-02-svarochisha/.intro: This is the second of the fourteen cosmic ages. Some scriptures simply say its ruler, Svarochisha, was the son of the fire god Agni, with no story attached. But one text, the Markandeya Purana, tells a richer tale: a devoted husband named Pravara is tricked by a spirit who takes his shape, and a romance follows through three generations, ending when a doe begs a man named Svarochis for mercy and then gives birth to the Manu of this age in an instant.

whoIsWho.name: Svarochisha Manu
whoIsWho.role: ruler of the second age; in one telling, born from a doe

whoIsWho.name: Pravara
whoIsWho.role: a faithful married priest whose story opens the tale

whoIsWho.name: Svarochis
whoIsWho.role: Pravara's radiant son, father of the Manu in this version

/manvantaras/manvantara-02-svarochisha/.whyItMatters: This age shows how the same ruler can have two completely different origin stories in different scriptures — one bare, one a full romance — and the corpus keeps both rather than picking a winner.

/manvantaras/manvantara-03-uttama/.intro: This is the third of the fourteen cosmic ages, and one of the least storied. Its ruler is Uttama, a son of the ancient king Priyavrata, but almost nothing happens here except administrative lists — who was king of the gods, which sages served — and different scriptures disagree on nearly every name. The one striking detail is that the seven wise sages of this age are said to be the reborn sons of the great sage Vashishtha, coming back to serve a second time.

whoIsWho.name: Uttama
whoIsWho.role: the Manu, or ruling ancestor, of this third age

whoIsWho.name: Vashishtha
whoIsWho.role: the sage whose seven sons from the first age are reborn as the sages here

/manvantaras/manvantara-03-uttama/.whyItMatters: This page is honest that some ages in the tradition are just name-lists with no surviving story — useful for seeing how thin the Puranic record can get.

/manvantaras/manvantara-04-tamasa/.intro: This is the fourth of the fourteen cosmic ages, ruled by a Manu named Tamasa. Like most of these early ages, its official records are just lists of names that disagree across scriptures. But one famous story is placed here: Gajendra, a great elephant king, is caught by the leg by a crocodile in a lake and struggles for years before finally calling out to God for help. Vishnu arrives riding his eagle Garuda, kills the crocodile, and saves the elephant.

whoIsWho.name: Tamasa
whoIsWho.role: the Manu, or ruling ancestor, of this fourth age

whoIsWho.name: Gajendra
whoIsWho.role: the elephant king seized by a crocodile in a forest lake

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: arrives on his eagle Garuda to save Gajendra

/manvantaras/manvantara-04-tamasa/.whyItMatters: The Gajendra story is one of the tradition's clearest teaching stories about giving up on your own strength and trusting God completely.

/manvantaras/manvantara-05-raivata/.intro: This is the fifth of the fourteen cosmic ages, ruled by a Manu named Raivata. Like the ages around it, the record is mostly lists of names. But the age lends its name to a famous story about time itself: a king called Kakudmi, who shares the name Raivata, takes his daughter Revati to see the creator god Brahma to find her a husband. While they wait through what feels like a short visit, millions of years pass on earth, and every suitor Kakudmi had in mind is long dead when they return.

whoIsWho.name: Raivata
whoIsWho.role: the Manu, or ruling ancestor, of this fifth age

whoIsWho.name: Kakudmi
whoIsWho.role: a later king who shares the name Raivata; father of Revati

whoIsWho.name: Revati
whoIsWho.role: Kakudmi's daughter, far taller than the people of her new age

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: the hero Brahma chooses as Revati's husband

/manvantaras/manvantara-05-raivata/.whyItMatters: The Kakudmi story is a striking old example of time passing at different speeds in different realms — the corpus flags that it belongs to a later king, not the Manu of this age.

/manvantaras/manvantara-06-chakshusha/.intro: This is the sixth and last cosmic age before our own, and it carries more stories than the ages before it because it sits right on the edge of our own history. In this age, the sage-pair Nara and Narayana are born, who will later be reborn as Arjuna and Krishna. Also born here are three sons of a devoted woman named Anasuya, who take partial birth from the gods Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. This age ends with the great flood story, in which Vishnu as a giant fish saves the first man of our own era.

whoIsWho.name: Chakshusha
whoIsWho.role: the Manu, or ruling ancestor, of this sixth age

whoIsWho.name: Nara and Narayana
whoIsWho.role: twin ascetic sages, later reborn as Arjuna and Krishna

whoIsWho.name: Anasuya
whoIsWho.role: a devoted wife whose sons carry the essence of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva

/manvantaras/manvantara-06-chakshusha/.whyItMatters: This age is the direct bridge into our own — its ending, a great flood, is also the beginning of the Vaivasvata age we are still living in.

/manvantaras/manvantara-08-savarni/.intro: This is the eighth cosmic age, and it hasn't happened yet — it lies far in the future, after our own current age ends. It carries one exciting piece of news: the king Bali, pushed down to the underworld by Vishnu's Dwarf form for claiming too much of the universe, is promised he will become the new king of the gods (Indra) in this future age, as a reward for his devotion. The scriptures also link this age to a king named Suratha, who loses his kingdom, worships the Goddess in the forest, and is reborn as its ruling ancestor.

whoIsWho.name: Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future Manu of this eighth age; in one telling, the reborn King Suratha

whoIsWho.name: Bali
whoIsWho.role: the generous demon-king promised the throne of the gods in this future age

whoIsWho.name: Vishnu
whoIsWho.role: appears as Sarvabhauma to hand the gods' throne over to Bali

/manvantaras/manvantara-08-savarni/.whyItMatters: This age answers a loose end from the Vamana-Bali story: it is where Bali finally gets his reward for keeping his word, even after losing his kingdom.

/manvantaras/manvantara-09-daksha-savarn.intro: This is the ninth cosmic age, still far in the future. Like most future ages, its scriptures give only a name-list of who will hold each important job — the ruling ancestor (Manu), the king of the gods (Indra), the seven sages — without telling any actual story. Its Manu is called Daksha-Savarni, said to be a son of the god Varuna, and its future king of the gods is named Adbhuta. No adventures are recorded for this age; it exists on paper as a roster waiting for its turn.

whoIsWho.name: Daksha-Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this ninth age

whoIsWho.name: Adbhuta
whoIsWho.role: the future king of the gods (Indra) for this age

/manvantaras/manvantara-09-daksha-savarn.whyItMatters: This page shows how honest the corpus tries to be: rather than invent a story where none survives, it simply says this age is still just a list of names waiting to happen.

/manvantaras/manvantara-10-brahma-savarn.intro: This is the tenth cosmic age, another one still to come. Its scriptures again give only a bare list of future office-holders: the ruling ancestor (Manu) will be called Brahma-Savarni, son of a man named Upasloka; the king of the gods will be named Sambhu; and Vishnu will appear in this age as Vishvaksena. No stories or events survive about what actually happens — only these names, and even they differ slightly between different scriptures.

whoIsWho.name: Brahma-Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this tenth age

whoIsWho.name: Vishvaksena
whoIsWho.role: the name Vishnu will take when he appears in this age

/manvantaras/manvantara-10-brahma-savarn.whyItMatters: Like its neighboring future ages, this page shows the tradition cataloguing a name-list for an age that hasn't happened yet, rather than inventing untold adventures.

/manvantaras/manvantara-11-dharma-savarn.intro: This is the eleventh cosmic age, still to come. Its future ruling ancestor (Manu) is named Dharma-Savarni, son of a sage named Ruci, and the scriptures say he is himself an earlier form of Vishnu's avatar for this age, named Dharmasetu — so the ruler and the divine helper of this age are one and the same being. Beyond that, the record is just a list of names, and the two main scriptures cannot even agree on who will be king of the gods in this age.

whoIsWho.name: Dharma-Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this eleventh age

whoIsWho.name: Dharmasetu
whoIsWho.role: Vishnu's future form for this age, identified with the Manu himself

/manvantaras/manvantara-11-dharma-savarn.whyItMatters: This is one of the few future ages where the Manu and Vishnu's avatar are described as linked, rather than as two separate figures.

/manvantaras/manvantara-12-rudra-savarni.intro: This is the twelfth cosmic age, still far in the future. Its ruling ancestor (Manu) will be called Rudra-Savarni, and Vishnu will appear in this age as an avatar named Svadhaman. As with the other future ages, no actual events are recorded — the scriptures give only the standard roster of who will hold each cosmic job, and even small details like exact names shift between texts.

whoIsWho.name: Rudra-Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this twelfth age

whoIsWho.name: Svadhaman
whoIsWho.role: the name Vishnu will take when he appears in this age

/manvantaras/manvantara-12-rudra-savarni.whyItMatters: This page continues the pattern of the future ages: a placeholder roster of names rather than a told story.

/manvantaras/manvantara-13-deva-savarni/.intro: This is the thirteenth cosmic age, still to come. It has two names for its future ruler: most scriptures call him Deva-Savarni, but one text, the Markandeya Purana, tells an actual story about a ruler it calls Raucya instead. In that story, a wandering sage named Ruci refuses to ever marry, believing family life only brings suffering, until his ancestors scold him for shirking his duty and Brahma orders him to marry and have a son who will become a future Manu. Scholars are unsure whether Raucya and Deva-Savarni are the same person.

whoIsWho.name: Deva-Savarni
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this thirteenth age, in most scriptures

whoIsWho.name: Ruci
whoIsWho.role: a sage who at first refuses to marry, in the story that may describe this age

whoIsWho.name: Raucya
whoIsWho.role: the son born to Ruci, possibly the same figure as Deva-Savarni

/manvantaras/manvantara-13-deva-savarni/.whyItMatters: This is one of the few future ages with an actual story attached, though the tradition itself is unsure whether it describes the ruler its other scriptures call Deva-Savarni.

/manvantaras/manvantara-14-indra-savarni.intro: This is the fourteenth and very last of the fourteen cosmic ages that make up one full day in the life of the god Brahma. Its future ruler, called Indra-Savarni or Bhautya, has a short birth story: his father, a stern and long-childless man named Bhuti, was away when the sacred fire at his hermitage went out. Bhuti's disciple prayed to the fire god Agni to relight it, and Agni granted that Bhuti would finally have a son — the future Manu of this last age. When this age ends, Brahma's whole cosmic Day closes, and the universe rests before the cycle begins again.

whoIsWho.name: Indra-Savarni (Bhautya)
whoIsWho.role: the future ruling ancestor (Manu) of this final age

whoIsWho.name: Bhuti
whoIsWho.role: Bhautya's long-childless father

whoIsWho.name: Agni
whoIsWho.role: the fire god who grants Bhuti's boon of a son

/manvantaras/manvantara-14-indra-savarni.whyItMatters: This age marks the very end of Brahma's cosmic Day — after it, everything dissolves into a Night of Brahma before creation starts fresh.

/lineages/ila-sudyumna/.intro: Ila, also called Sudyumna, is one of the strangest figures in Hindu genealogy: a child of the ancestor Manu who changes between being a man and a woman. Born as a daughter after a sacrifice goes wrong, Ila is turned into a son, but wanders into a forest grove near Mount Meru where Shiva has decreed any man who enters becomes a woman. As a woman again, Ila is loved by a being named Budha and gives birth to Pururavas, the first king of the Lunar dynasty. A later compromise lets Sudyumna live as a man one month and a woman the next, until finally giving up the throne.

whoIsWho.name: Ila (Sudyumna)
whoIsWho.role: a child of Manu who changes between being a man and a woman

whoIsWho.name: Budha
whoIsWho.role: loves Ila while she is in her female form; father of Pururavas

whoIsWho.name: Pururavas
whoIsWho.role: the son born to Ila, first king of the Lunar dynasty

/lineages/ila-sudyumna/.whyItMatters: Ila/Sudyumna is the one point where Hindu tradition's two great royal family trees — the Solar and Lunar lines — actually connect, since this Solar-born child becomes, as a woman, the mother of the first Lunar king.

/stories/ramayana/2-ayodhya-kanda/.intro: This is the second book of the Ramayana. King Dashratha wants to crown his son Rama as the next king, but his wife Kaikeyi, talked into it by her servant Manthara, calls in two old promises: her own son Bharata must be crowned instead, and Rama must go to the forest for fourteen years. Rama accepts without anger, because a father's word must be kept. His wife Sita and brother Lakshmana insist on going with him. Heartbroken, King Dashratha dies of grief. Bharata refuses the throne his mother won for him and rules only as a caretaker, placing Rama's sandals on the throne until he returns.

whoIsWho.name: Rama
whoIsWho.role: the prince who accepts fourteen years of exile without complaint

whoIsWho.name: Kaikeyi
whoIsWho.role: Dashratha's wife, who demands Rama's exile using two old promises

whoIsWho.name: Manthara
whoIsWho.role: Kaikeyi's servant, who convinces her to make the demands

whoIsWho.name: Bharata
whoIsWho.role: Kaikeyi's son, who refuses the throne and rules only as caretaker

/stories/ramayana/2-ayodhya-kanda/.whyItMatters: This book is Hindu tradition's great study of keeping your word even when it costs you everything, and of a brother who refuses power that isn't rightfully his.

/stories/ramayana/3-aranya-kanda/.intro: This is the third book of the Ramayana, covering years of forest exile for Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana. A demon princess named Shurpanakha falls for Rama, and when she attacks Sita out of jealousy, Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears. She runs to her brother Khara, who attacks with an army and is destroyed by Rama alone. Shurpanakha then goes to her other brother, the demon king Ravana, and describes Sita's beauty. Ravana tricks the couple with a magical golden deer, luring both brothers away, then kidnaps Sita. The giant vulture Jatayu tries to save her and is mortally wounded fighting Ravana.

whoIsWho.name: Shurpanakha
whoIsWho.role: a demon princess whose mutilation sparks the whole war

whoIsWho.name: Khara
whoIsWho.role: Shurpanakha's brother, killed along with his army by Rama alone

whoIsWho.name: Ravana
whoIsWho.role: the demon king who kidnaps Sita using a magical deer as a trick

whoIsWho.name: Jatayu
whoIsWho.role: an aged vulture who fights Ravana to try to save Sita

/stories/ramayana/3-aranya-kanda/.whyItMatters: This book contains the central turning point of the whole epic — Sita's kidnapping — which is what makes the rest of the story, and the eventual war, happen.

/stories/ramayana/4-kishkindha-kanda/.intro: This is the fourth book of the Ramayana. Searching for Sita, Rama meets the monkey hero Hanuman and allies with the exiled monkey prince Sugriva, driven out of his kingdom by his stronger brother Vali. In exchange for help finding Sita, Rama kills Vali by shooting him from hiding during a fight with Sugriva — an act some in the story itself call unfair, though Rama explains his reasons. Sugriva becomes king but forgets his promise until Lakshmana angrily reminds him. Finally, armies of monkeys are sent in every direction, and the southern group, led by Hanuman, learns from a dying vulture exactly where Sita is held.

whoIsWho.name: Sugriva
whoIsWho.role: an exiled monkey prince who allies with Rama to win back his throne

whoIsWho.name: Vali
whoIsWho.role: Sugriva's powerful brother, killed by Rama from hiding

whoIsWho.name: Hanuman
whoIsWho.role: the monkey hero who becomes Rama's most devoted helper

/stories/ramayana/4-kishkindha-kanda/.whyItMatters: This book sets up the alliance and search that makes finding Sita possible, and includes one of the epic's most debated moments — whether Rama was right to kill Vali by stealth.

/stories/ramayana/5-sundara-kanda/.intro: This is the fifth book of the Ramayana, and the only one where Rama is not the main character — it belongs to Hanuman. The monkey hero leaps across the ocean to the island kingdom of Lanka, sneaks into the city, and finds Sita held captive in a garden, refusing to give in to the demon king Ravana. Hanuman gives her Rama's ring as proof he is a real messenger, and she gives him her jewel to carry back. Before leaving, Hanuman lets himself be captured, and when the demons set his tail on fire, he uses it to burn down much of the city.

whoIsWho.name: Hanuman
whoIsWho.role: the monkey hero who finds Sita and burns down part of Lanka

whoIsWho.name: Sita
whoIsWho.role: held captive in Ravana's garden, refusing to submit

whoIsWho.name: Ravana
whoIsWho.role: the demon king holding Sita prisoner

/stories/ramayana/5-sundara-kanda/.whyItMatters: This is the most independently loved and recited book of the whole epic, because it is the story of an impossible task — finding Sita — finally being achieved.

/stories/characters/bhishma/.intro: Bhishma is the grand old warrior of the Mahabharata, uncle and guardian to both feuding sides of the family. As a young prince named Devavrata, he gave up his own right to the throne and swore never to marry, just so his father could remarry — a vow so extreme the gods rewarded him with the power to choose the moment of his own death. Because of his loyalty to the throne, he fights for the Kauravas in the great war, even though he loves the Pandavas. On the tenth day, he lets himself be struck down by a wall of arrows, but delays his death for weeks to teach the dying wisdom of dharma.

whoIsWho.name: Bhishma
whoIsWho.role: the celibate warrior-patriarch who chooses the timing of his own death

whoIsWho.name: Devavrata
whoIsWho.role: Bhishma's birth name, before his terrible vow

whoIsWho.name: Shikhandin
whoIsWho.role: a warrior Bhishma refuses to fight, letting Arjuna strike him down

/stories/characters/bhishma/.whyItMatters: Bhishma's story is about the cost of an extreme vow: his sacrifice secures one throne but unravels his whole family, and his last words teach the very lessons he could not follow while alive.

/stories/characters/drona/.intro: Drona is the brahmin warrior-teacher who trains both the Kauravas and the Pandavas in archery. Poor and humiliated after his childhood friend, King Drupada, refuses to share his kingdom as promised, Drona becomes royal teacher at Hastinapura and makes Arjuna his favorite student. When a tribal boy named Ekalavya secretly becomes an even better archer by training alone, Drona demands the boy's thumb as a teaching fee, crippling him, just to keep Arjuna the best. Drona later gets his revenge on Drupada, but Drupada's children are born to destroy him. During the war, Drona is tricked into laying down his weapons by a false report of his son's death, then beheaded unarmed.

whoIsWho.name: Drona
whoIsWho.role: the brahmin master of weapons who teaches both warring families

whoIsWho.name: Drupada
whoIsWho.role: Drona's childhood friend turned enemy, whose humiliation starts the feud

whoIsWho.name: Ekalavya
whoIsWho.role: a self-taught archer whose thumb Drona demands as a cruel fee

/stories/characters/drona/.whyItMatters: Drona's story is one of the epic's harshest lessons about favoritism and loyalty to the wrong side — his gifts as a teacher are matched by his cruelty to a student he never wanted to have.

/stories/characters/balarama/.intro: Balarama is Krishna's older brother, a mighty hero who carries a plough as his weapon and is believed to be an incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha. He grows up alongside Krishna, kills demons as a boy, and later becomes the mace-fighting teacher of both Bhima and Duryodhana. When the Kurukshetra war breaks out, Balarama refuses to fight for either side because he loves both families, and goes on pilgrimage instead. Years later, when Krishna's own clan destroys itself in a drunken brawl, Balarama sits calmly under a tree, enters deep meditation, and lets his body go — a great white serpent is seen leaving his mouth and gliding into the sea.

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's elder brother, believed to be the serpent Shesha in human form

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: Balarama's younger brother, alongside whom he grows up

whoIsWho.name: Bhima and Duryodhana
whoIsWho.role: the two mace-fighting students Balarama trains

/stories/characters/balarama/.whyItMatters: Balarama shows a different path through the great war than Krishna — refusing violence between kin — and his peaceful, serpent-revealing death marks the traditional start of Kali Yuga.

/stories/mahabharata/16-mausala-parva/.intro: This is the sixteenth book of the Mahabharata, and the bleakest. Thirty-six years after the great war, two old curses catch up with Krishna's own clan, the Yadavas. Sages once cursed that a prank would produce an iron club that would destroy the whole clan; ground to powder and thrown into the sea, it grows into sharp reeds on the shore. At a drunken festival, an argument turns violent, and the Yadavas grab those reeds — which turn into deadly clubs in their hands — and kill each other almost to the last man. Balarama then quietly dies in meditation, and soon after Krishna is mistaken for a deer and shot in the foot by a hunter.

whoIsWho.name: Krishna
whoIsWho.role: dies after being mistaken for a deer and shot by a hunter's arrow

whoIsWho.name: Balarama
whoIsWho.role: Krishna's brother, who dies peacefully in meditation just before him

whoIsWho.name: Jara
whoIsWho.role: the hunter whose arrow strikes and kills Krishna by accident

/stories/mahabharata/16-mausala-parva/.whyItMatters: Krishna's death here traditionally marks the end of the Dvapara age and the start of Kali Yuga, the current age — one of the most important turning points on the whole timeline.

/stories/mahabharata/17-mahaprasthanika-.intro: This is the seventeenth book of the Mahabharata, one of its shortest. After Krishna's death and the destruction of his clan, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi give up their kingdom and walk toward the Himalayas to die, taking only the clothes on their backs. A stray dog joins them and follows the whole way. One by one, starting with Draupadi, each Pandava collapses and dies on the mountain, each for a different personal flaw. Only Yudhishthira keeps walking, with no fault to weigh him down. When Indra offers to carry him to heaven, Yudhishthira refuses to leave the dog behind — and it reveals itself to be the god of righteousness, testing him one last time.

whoIsWho.name: Yudhishthira
whoIsWho.role: the only Pandava brother who reaches heaven without dying on the way

whoIsWho.name: Draupadi
whoIsWho.role: the shared wife of all five brothers, the first to fall

whoIsWho.name: Dharma
whoIsWho.role: the god of righteousness, disguised as the loyal dog throughout the journey

/stories/mahabharata/17-mahaprasthanika-.whyItMatters: This book's final test — choosing loyalty to a humble dog over a ride straight to heaven — is one of the clearest statements in the epic that compassion matters more than reward.

/cosmology/kalpa-and-pralaya/.intro: This page explains two of the biggest units of time in Hindu tradition: the kalpa, one full day in the life of the god Brahma (4.32 billion years), and pralaya, the dissolving of the universe that follows. There are four kinds of dissolution, from the everyday death of ordinary living things, to the nightly rest that ends each of Brahma's cosmic days, all the way up to the total collapse of everything into raw formless matter at the end of Brahma's whole life, and finally the personal, permanent freedom of one soul reaching liberation.

whoIsWho.name: Narayana (Vishnu)
whoIsWho.role: sleeps through each cosmic night resting on the serpent Shesha

whoIsWho.name: Markandeya
whoIsWho.role: a sage granted a vision of the flood, floating at the edge of dissolution

/cosmology/kalpa-and-pralaya/.whyItMatters: This page is the key to understanding phrases used across the site like "Day of Brahma" — it explains exactly what dissolves, what survives, and how it all starts again.

/cosmology/brahma-lifetime/.intro: This page maps out the entire lifespan of the god Brahma, the creator, which lasts 311.04 trillion human years in total. Tradition says we are just past the halfway point of his life, in the very first day of his 51st year out of 100. Each of his days is a kalpa (4.32 billion years), made of fourteen ages called Manvantaras, and we live in the seventh of those fourteen. When Brahma's hundred-year life finally ends, everything, even Brahma himself, dissolves back into formless raw matter, before a brand new Brahma is born and the whole cycle starts again.

whoIsWho.name: Brahma
whoIsWho.role: the creator god whose 311-trillion-year lifespan structures all of cosmic time

/cosmology/brahma-lifetime/.whyItMatters: This page gives the single biggest scale on the site's cosmic clock — it shows that even a god as vast as Brahma has a lifespan, and our current age is a tiny sliver near its middle.

/beings/twelve-devasura-battles/.intro: One ancient text, the Matsya Purana, lists exactly twelve great wars between the gods (devas) and the demons (asuras), giving each one a name. Some of these are famous stories you can read elsewhere on this site, like the churning of the ocean for the nectar of immortality, or Vishnu's Man-Lion form killing the tyrant Hiranyakashipu. But three of the twelve wars are just names on the list — their stories were apparently lost even by the time this text was written, so nobody today knows what happened in them.

whoIsWho.name: Narasimha, Vamana, Varaha
whoIsWho.role: three of Vishnu's animal-and-dwarf forms, each with its own war on the list

whoIsWho.name: Shukra
whoIsWho.role: the demons' teacher, who seeks new powers from Shiva after twelve defeats

/beings/twelve-devasura-battles/.whyItMatters: This page is a rare case of an ancient Hindu text actually counting and numbering its own war-stories, and it honestly admits that some of those stories have been lost over time.

/stories/nala-damayanti/.intro: This is the story of King Nala and Princess Damayanti, told to comfort Yudhishthira during his own forest exile in the Mahabharata. Nala and Damayanti fall in love just from hearing about each other, and Damayanti chooses Nala over four gods in disguise at her own bridal ceremony, noticing that gods never blink, sweat, or let their feet touch the ground. Furious a mortal beat them to her, the demon of the current age, Kali, waits twelve years for Nala to slip up, then possesses him and rigs a dice game so Nala loses his kingdom. Nala abandons Damayanti in the forest, and the two suffer years apart before reuniting.

whoIsWho.name: Nala
whoIsWho.role: a king who loses everything to a rigged dice game while possessed by the demon Kali

whoIsWho.name: Damayanti
whoIsWho.role: Nala's wife, who proves her devotion through years of hardship

whoIsWho.name: Kali
whoIsWho.role: the demon of the current age, who possesses Nala out of jealousy

/stories/nala-damayanti/.whyItMatters: This story mirrors the Mahabharata's own dice-game disaster and is told specifically to give Yudhishthira hope that even total ruin by gambling can be reversed.
